Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — How do I learn it?
English: How do I learn it?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — How do I learn it?
English: Take one verse at a time, listening and repeating rather than reading. The Practice screen has all seven with a recording against each, and a repeat button. Play a line, say it with the reciter, and move on when it holds. Most people need days, not minutes.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — How do I learn it?
English: Until you have it, say what you know and keep going. Nobody expects a first-week Muslim to have memorised it, and the prayer you pray while learning is still your prayer.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What am I actually saying?
English: What am I actually saying?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What am I actually saying?
English: It opens by praising God as the Lord of everything and the source of mercy, then turns and speaks to Him directly: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. The rest is a request: guide us along the straight path. It is a prayer for guidance, said before anything else is asked for.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What is Al-Fatihah?
English: What is Al-Fatihah?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What is Al-Fatihah?
English: The opening chapter of the Qur’an, seven short verses. Its name means "The Opening". It is the most repeated passage in the world: every Muslim says it in every unit of every prayer, which for most people is seventeen times a day.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — Why does every prayer need it?
English: Why does every prayer need it?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — Why does every prayer need it?
English: Because without it there is no prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does not recite Al-Fatihah in their prayer, their prayer is invalid. Of everything a new Muslim could memorise, this is the one that changes what they are able to do today.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What can I ask about?
English: What can I ask about?

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What can I ask about?
English: Any time except the times when prayer is held off, and about anything you genuinely have a choice in: a job, a move, a marriage, something smaller. Not about whether to do something already settled as right or wrong; there is nothing to ask about there.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What do I say?
English: What do I say?

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What do I say?
English: Said after the two rakʿahs. Where it says “this matter”, name the thing you are deciding.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What is istikhara?
English: What is istikhara?

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What is istikhara?
English: Two rakʿahs and a duʿa, prayed when you have a decision to make. Jabir reported that the Prophet ﷺ taught it for every matter the way he taught a surah of the Qur’an, which tells you how ordinary it was meant to be, and how often.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What sign should I expect?
English: What sign should I expect?

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What sign should I expect?
English: This is the part people are told wrong. The duʿa asks God, if the thing is good for you, to bring it about and make it easy, and if it is bad for you, to turn it away and turn you away from it. It does not promise a sign, a dream or a feeling. You pray, and then you decide, and what follows is the answer.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What sign should I expect?
English: You still have to think, ask people who know, and weigh it up. Istikhara goes alongside that, not instead of it.

Where it appears: Asr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Asr.

Where it appears: Asr — Turn to your left
English: That is Asr complete.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Know what you are saying
English: Know what you are saying

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Know what you are saying
English: Becoming Muslim is one sentence, said and meant. Before you say it, be clear on both halves: that worship belongs to Allah alone and nothing shares that with Him, and that Muhammad ﷺ was sent by Him to convey how.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Know what you are saying
English: It has to be meant. Saying the words to please someone else, or to marry, does not make a person Muslim.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: Say it

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: Say it aloud, in Arabic if you can manage it. If the Arabic is beyond you today, say it in your own language and mean it, then learn the Arabic, because you will say it in every prayer for the rest of your life.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: You are Muslim from the moment you say it and mean it. Nobody has to be there, and no imam has to be present.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: Getting it written down is a separate question, and worth doing when you can. A mosque or Islamic centre can record it and give you a certificate. Not because your Islam needs one, but because other people's paperwork sometimes does.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: These are two different things and the app keeps them apart on purpose. Whether you are Muslim is settled between you and Allah the moment you say it and mean it, and both answers cited here say so plainly, one of them in the words "Islam is a matter that is between a person and his Lord". Whether a registrar, a mosque, a Hajj visa office or a marriage contract will take your word for it later is a paperwork question with a paperwork answer. Historically witnesses were asked for in Muslim courts because inheritance and marriage law followed a person's religion, which is where the idea that they are required comes from. If you are not ready to walk into a mosque, that is fine. None of this expires, and the certificate is available whenever you want it.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — You are Muslim
English: You are Muslim

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — You are Muslim
English: That is it. Nothing else is required of you in this moment, and nothing you did before it is held against you. Becoming Muslim wipes what came before.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — You are Muslim
English: You do not need to change your name. You do not need to tell anyone today. Take a full wash when you can, which is recommended for someone who has just become Muslim, and then learn wudu and the prayer, in that order, without rushing.

Where it appears: Clothing — Is this only about women?
English: Is this only about women?

Where it appears: Clothing — Is this only about women?
English: The instruction to lower the gaze and guard modesty is given to men first and then to women, in consecutive verses. That order is worth noticing: modesty in Islam is not a set of rules aimed only at women, and men have their own covering to observe.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for men?
English: What does it mean for men?

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for men?
English: Cover at least from the navel to the knee, keep clothing loose enough not to be revealing, and avoid pure silk and gold jewellery, which the Prophet ﷺ restricted for men. In ordinary Western dress this changes very little in practice.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: What does it mean for women?

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The Qur’an instructs believing women to guard their modesty, to draw their head-coverings over the chest, and to draw their outer garments about them. The commonly taught result is loose clothing covering the body, with the head covered, in front of men outside the immediate family.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: Whether the face and hands must also be covered is a long-standing point of scholarly difference, not a settled question.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: This note used to weigh a majority against a minority, and that count does not hold in either direction. Dorar’s Encyclopedia of Fiqh calls covering the face the view of the majority of scholars, while summaries written from inside the Hanafi and Maliki schools present the opposite as the common position. So the schools are named below rather than counted. You will meet Muslims on both sides who are each following scholarship they trust, and the detail of any one school is worth hearing from someone qualified rather than reading in a summary.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The face and hands are what ordinarily shows, so covering them is not required in itself, though the school still calls for covering where there is a real fear of harassment.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The face is not itself among the parts that must be covered, but the position recorded in the school from early on is that it is covered in front of men a woman could marry, because of the harm of not doing so.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The school carries two positions, and the more predominant of them is that the face is covered in front of men a woman could marry.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The position the school takes as most correct is that the face and hands are covered in front of men a woman could marry.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: Nobody has the right to pressure you, and starting is often gradual. If covering would put you in danger or out you before you are ready, that is a real circumstance to discuss with someone knowledgeable rather than a rule you are breaking.

Where it appears: Clothing — What is the idea behind it?
English: What is the idea behind it?

Where it appears: Clothing — What is the idea behind it?
English: The Qur’an speaks about clothing as something given for covering and for adornment: both, not one at the expense of the other. Islam is not against looking good. The instructions that follow are about modesty in public, not about drabness.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Add a short surah; Asr — Add a short surah; Tahajjud — Add a short surah; Qiyam al-Layl — Add a short surah; Witr — Add a short surah; Istikhara — Add a short surah; The prayer of repentance — Add a short surah
English: After Al-Fatihah, recite another short surah quietly. Al-Ikhlas is four verses and is where most people start:

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Dhuhr.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Final sitting; Asr — Final sitting; Maghrib — Final sitting; Isha — Final sitting
English: Say the takbir and sit again. This time slide your left foot across under you to the right and sit on the ground, right foot still upright. Rest your left hand on your left knee and your right hand on your right thigh, raise your right index finger, and say:

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Recite Al-Fatihah; Asr — Recite Al-Fatihah; Maghrib — Recite Al-Fatihah; Isha — Recite Al-Fatihah; Tahajjud — Recite Al-Fatihah; Qiyam al-Layl — Recite Al-Fatihah; Witr — Recite Al-Fatihah; Istikhara — Recite Al-Fatihah; The prayer of repentance — Recite Al-Fatihah
English: Recite the opening chapter of the Qur’an quietly, so only you can hear it.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Sit for tashahhud; Asr — Sit for tashahhud; Maghrib — Sit for tashahhud; Isha — Sit for tashahhud
English: Sit for tashahhud

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Stand for the fourth rakʿah; Asr — Stand for the fourth rakʿah; Isha — Stand for the fourth rakʿah
English: Stand for the fourth rakʿah

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Stand for the third rakʿah; Asr — Stand for the third rakʿah; Maghrib — Stand for the third rakʿah; Isha — Stand for the third rakʿah
English: Stand for the third rakʿah

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Stand for the third rakʿah; Asr — Stand for the third rakʿah; Maghrib — Stand for the third rakʿah; Isha — Stand for the third rakʿah
English: Rise to standing, saying the takbir and raising your hands to shoulder level as you rise, then rest your right hand over your left forearm again.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — Turn to your left
English: That is Dhuhr complete.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What are the four before and after?
English: What are the four before and after?

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What are the four before and after?
English: Dhuhr carries the largest voluntary escort of the five: four rakʿahs before it and more after. Keeping them was tied to a promise no other rawatib carries in these words.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What if I am at work?
English: What if I am at work?

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What if I am at work?
English: Dhuhr is four silent rakʿahs — a few minutes in any clean, quiet corner. If the window closes on you anyway, the page on missing a prayer walks through catching it up.

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What is Dhuhr?
English: What is Dhuhr?

Where it appears: Dhuhr — What is Dhuhr?
English: Four rakʿahs once the sun has passed its height — the first prayer of the working day, prayed silently, and one of the five the Prophet ﷺ compared to a river at your door.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — Do I have to take a new name?
English: Do I have to take a new name?

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — Do I have to take a new name?
English:
Becoming Muslim does not require a new name. Most names are simply names, and a name that means something ordinary in another language is not a problem to be solved. Plenty of Muslims you will meet have the name they were born with.

Some people do choose one, and that is theirs to choose. It is a preference, not a step.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — So why do people think you must?
English: So why do people think you must?

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — So why do people think you must?
English: The Prophet ﷺ did change some people’s names — where a name carried a meaning worth leaving behind. What is worth noticing is how one of those went: he suggested a man called Ḥazn, which means something like grief, be called Sahl instead, meaning ease. The man said he would not change the name his father gave him, and he kept it.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — So why do people think you must?
English: That narration is in Bukhari and it is not presented as disobedience. It is the reason to be careful with anybody who tells you this is required.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What about my family name?
English: What about my family name?

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What about my family name?
English: This part is not a preference. The Qur’an instructs that people be called by their fathers’ names, and converts keep their family name for the same reason — your lineage is not something Islam asks you to drop, and cutting yourself off from it is the opposite of what is asked.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What if I want one anyway?
English: What if I want one anyway?

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What if I want one anyway?
English: Then take one, and there is no ceremony involved. You do not need permission, a witness, or a legal change, and nothing about your becoming Muslim depends on it. Many people use one among Muslim friends and their own everywhere else, which is not a contradiction.

Where it appears: Do I have to change my name? — What if I want one anyway?
English: If somebody at a mosque starts calling you by a name you did not choose, you are allowed to say you prefer your own.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Then is it wrong to pray where people can see me?
English: Then is it wrong to pray where people can see me?

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Then is it wrong to pray where people can see me?
English: No, and this is the question converts actually have rather than the one the topic is usually written for. Praying at work, fasting in front of colleagues, saying you cannot drink — all of that is visible, and none of it is riyāʾ, because you would be doing it in an empty room. Riyāʾ is not the presence of an audience. It is the audience being the reason.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Then is it wrong to pray where people can see me?
English: Much of the obligatory worship is public by design. The prayer is in congregation, zakat is collected, hajj is a crowd. A religion that treated being seen as the problem could not ask for any of it.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What does this look like for me now?
English: The first year has an unusual amount of announcing in it — telling family, telling friends, being asked about it constantly. Saying what you now believe is not riyāʾ; it is answering a question. The place to watch is smaller and quieter: praying longer because somebody is in the room, mentioning the fast that nobody asked about. Small enough that nobody else would ever notice, which is the point.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What if the thought comes in the middle?
English: What if the thought comes in the middle?

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What if the thought comes in the middle?
English: It will. You are halfway through a prayer and notice that someone is watching and that part of you is glad. Noticing it is not the same as having acted on it — the thought arriving is what shayṭān does, and being annoyed by it is a sign the intention is alive rather than gone. Carry on with the prayer. Do not abandon a good deed because the thought showed up in it; that hands the whole thing over for the price of a distraction.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What is riyāʾ?
English: What is riyāʾ?

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — What is riyāʾ?
English: It is doing an act of worship so that people see you doing it. The narration is blunt about the exchange: whoever makes his deed heard of, Allah will make him heard of; whoever does it to be seen, Allah will show him up. You asked to be looked at, and you will be — which is exactly the payment, and the whole of it.

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Why is it treated so seriously?
English: Why is it treated so seriously?

Where it appears: Doing it to be seen — Why is it treated so seriously?
English: Because of what it does to the deed itself. In a ḥadīth qudsī, Allah says He is the least in need of a partner: whoever does something and associates another with Him in it, He leaves him and the one he associated. The deed is not reduced. It is handed over to the person you did it for.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is dhikr?
English: What is dhikr?

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is dhikr?
English: Dhikr means remembrance: short phrases repeated through the day. Subḥāna-llāh (glory be to God), al-ḥamdu li-llāh (all praise is God’s), Allāhu akbar (God is greatest). The Qur’an says hearts settle by the remembrance of God, and that is closer to what it does than anything a description manages.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is duʿa?
English: What is duʿa?

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is duʿa?
English: Duʿa is simply asking God for something. It has no set form, no required language and no appointed time. The Qur’an says He is near and answers the one who calls. You can make duʿa in English, in your own words, in the car, and it is the same duʿa.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is duʿa?
English: You do not need Arabic for this. The memorised duʿas are worth learning because they are the Prophet’s ﷺ wording, not because your own words would be rejected.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — Where do I start?
English: Where do I start?

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — Where do I start?
English: Pick one phrase and one moment, such as waking or the walk to work. The Everyday duʿas screen has short ones with the Arabic, how it sounds and what it means. The shortest is a single word, which is a deliberate place to begin rather than a compromise.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — Why does it matter so much?
English: The Prophet ﷺ compared the person who remembers their Lord to the living, and the one who does not to the dead. He also said that whoever says subḥāna-llāhi wa bi-ḥamdih a hundred times in a day has their sins forgiven though they were like the foam of the sea.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — Why does it matter so much?; ʿAsr — Why does it matter so much?
English: Why does it matter so much?

Where it appears: Eid — What do people do before it?
English: What do people do before it?

Where it appears: Eid — What do people do before it?
English: Wash, put on the best clothes they own, and go. On Eid al-Fitr specifically the Prophet ﷺ would eat something — dates — before leaving, which is worth knowing because on every other festival morning you might assume you were meant to be fasting. You are not; fasting on the two Eids is not done.

Where it appears: Eid — What if I have nobody to spend it with?
English: What if I have nobody to spend it with?

Where it appears: Eid — What if I have nobody to spend it with?
English:
This is the hardest day of the year for a lot of converts, and it is worth saying plainly rather than leaving you to discover it. A family day is a hard day to have no family in.

Go to the prayer. Mosques are at their most welcoming that morning and somebody will almost certainly invite you to eat — if nobody does, it is fair to say to a person there that it is your first Eid. That sentence tends to end with you at a table.

Where it appears: Eid — What if I have nobody to spend it with?
English: Plan it a few days ahead rather than on the morning. Eid arranged in advance is a different day from Eid improvised at 9am.

Where it appears: Eid — What is Eid?
English: What is Eid?

Where it appears: Eid — What is Eid?
English:
There are two, and only two. **Eid al-Fitr** is the morning after Ramadan ends. **Eid al-Adha** falls about ten weeks later, during the days of Hajj. Both begin with a prayer shortly after sunrise, and the rest of the day is food and family.

They are not solemn. People wear their best clothes, children get money, and the mosque is fuller than you have ever seen it.

Where it appears: Eid — What is the Eid prayer like?
English: What is the Eid prayer like?

Where it appears: Eid — What is the Eid prayer like?
English:
Short, and unlike the daily prayers in two ways: it is two rakʿah with several extra **Allāhu akbar** said before the recitation, and the talk comes AFTER the prayer rather than before it. There is no adhān and no iqāmah for it.

If you do not know when the extra takbīrs come, watch the row in front and raise your hands when they do.

Where it appears: Eid — When exactly is it?
English: When exactly is it?

Where it appears: Eid — When exactly is it?
English: Ask your local mosque, and ask a day or two before. The month begins by sighting the new moon, so the date is not settled until it is — and mosques in the same city sometimes differ by a day. This app deliberately does not tell you, because a calculated date is wrong often enough to matter here.

Where it appears: Eid — When exactly is it?
English: If two mosques near you announce different days, that is an old and ordinary disagreement. Follow the one you pray with.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Are manners really part of it?
English: Are manners really part of it?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Are manners really part of it?
English: Character sits at the centre rather than the edge. The Prophet ﷺ, described in the Qur’an as being of great character, taught that the best of people are those with the best manners, and the people who lived with him said he never used foul or crude language.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Is there a summary?
English: Is there a summary?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Is there a summary?
English: The Prophet ﷺ tied belief directly to behaviour: whoever believes in God and the Last Day should not harm their neighbour, should be generous to their guest, and should say something good or stay quiet. Neighbours, guests, and how you speak. That is a large share of daily life.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What about talking about people?
English: What about talking about people?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What about talking about people?
English: The Qur’an forbids mocking others, assuming the worst, spying, and talking about people behind their backs, in two consecutive verses. Backbiting is treated as a serious wrong, not a small one, and it is the habit most people find hardest to drop.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What do I do when I am angry?
English: What do I do when I am angry?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What do I do when I am angry?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said the strong person is not the one who overpowers others, but the one who controls himself when angry. It is a redefinition rather than a rule, and it comes up more often than most of the rules do.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What is the measure of it?
English: What is the measure of it?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What is the measure of it?
English: One of the shortest things the Prophet ﷺ said and one of the hardest: none of you truly believes until he wants for his brother what he wants for himself. It is the test to apply when a situation is not covered by anything you have learned yet.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What is the measure of it?
English: You will get things wrong, in front of people, for a while. Everyone did. Being embarrassed about it is not a sign you are doing badly.

English: This part is sunnah, not required. A prayer of Al-Fatihah alone is a complete prayer, so if you do not know one yet, carry on to the bow.

English: After Al-Fatihah, recite another short surah aloud. Al-Ikhlas is four verses and is where most people start:

English: Bow

Where it appears: Fajr — Bow; Dhuhr — Bow; Asr — Bow; Maghrib — Bow; Isha — Bow; Tahajjud — Bow; Qiyam al-Layl — Bow; Witr — Bow; Istikhara — Bow; The prayer of repentance — Bow
English: Raise your hands again as you say the takbir, then bow with a straight back, hands gripping your knees, eyes down. Once settled, say:

Where it appears: Fajr — Bow; Dhuhr — Bow; Asr — Bow; Maghrib — Bow; Isha — Bow; Tahajjud — Bow; Qiyam al-Layl — Bow; Witr — Bow; Istikhara — Bow; The prayer of repentance — Bow
English: Settle in each position before you move to the next. This is the thing the Prophet ﷺ sent a man back to repeat his prayer for, three times over.

Where it appears: Fajr — Bow; Dhuhr — Bow; Asr — Bow; Maghrib — Bow; Isha — Bow; Tahajjud — Bow; Qiyam al-Layl — Bow; Witr — Bow; Istikhara — Bow; The prayer of repentance — Bow
English: He told him: bow until you are at rest bowing, then rise until you are standing straight, then prostrate until you are at rest prostrating, then sit until you are at rest sitting, and do that through the whole prayer. Speed is the most common fault in a new Muslim's prayer and the easiest to fix.

Where it appears: Fajr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Fajr.

English: Face the qibla and intend

Where it appears: Fajr — Face the qibla and intend; Dhuhr — Face the qibla and intend; Asr — Face the qibla and intend; Maghrib — Face the qibla and intend; Isha — Face the qibla and intend; Tahajjud — Face the qibla and intend; Qiyam al-Layl — Face the qibla and intend; Witr — Face the qibla and intend; Istikhara — Face the qibla and intend; The prayer of repentance — Face the qibla and intend
English: The intention is a thought, not a sentence. You do not need to say it out loud.

English: It is not — the fast itself is the same, dawn to sunset, and it begins with the same intention. What differs is that you can stop. A voluntary fast can be broken partway through without owing anything, which is not true of Ramadan, and that alone makes it a reasonable thing to attempt on a working day.

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — How should I start?
English: How should I start?

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — How should I start?
English:
One Monday. Not a schedule, not a commitment, not a fast you have announced. Do one, see what it is like on a normal day with a normal job, and decide afterwards.

If it goes badly, that is information rather than failure, and nothing about it is recorded anywhere.

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — How should I start?
English: Do not start the week you also start praying five times. One new thing at a time is how either of them lasts.

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — Which days do people fast?
English: Which days do people fast?

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — Which days do people fast?
English: A few, and they are ordinary rather than obscure. The easiest to start with are the weekly ones, because they need no calendar at all.

Where it appears: Fasting outside Ramadan — Which days do people fast?
English: This app will not tell you the date of ʿĀshūrāʾ or ʿArafah. Those depend on the moon being sighted, and a calculated date is wrong often enough that it would be a bad thing to be confident about. Ask your mosque in the week beforehand.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Breaking fast alone — is that even Ramadan?
English: Breaking fast alone — is that even Ramadan?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Breaking fast alone — is that even Ramadan?
English:
An iftar for one — a date, a glass of water, a plate you made yourself in a quiet kitchen — is a full iftar, witnessed by the One you kept the fast for. The duʿa at breaking the fast is in this app’s Duʿa tab, and the moment belongs to you either way.

It is still worth saying: this is the loneliest recurring moment of a solo Ramadan, and it does not have to stay solo.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Is it supposed to feel this strange?
English: Is it supposed to feel this strange?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Is it supposed to feel this strange?
English:
Ramadan is built as a shared month — shared pre-dawn meals, shared sunsets, whole cities changing rhythm. Keeping it alone, in a place running on its ordinary rhythm, is genuinely harder than keeping it surrounded by people who are also hungry. If your first Ramadan feels like swimming against a current, that is the situation, not a fault in your fasting.

The fast itself is exactly as valid alone as in Makkah. Nothing about other people’s participation is a condition of yours.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What do I say at work or school?
English: What do I say at work or school?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What do I say at work or school?
English:
You owe nobody an announcement, and you are hiding nothing shameful — both are true at once, and you get to pick your point on that line. Many people simply decline lunch with “I’m good, thanks.” Saying “I’m fasting — it’s Ramadan” is also a complete answer, and most colleagues respond with curiosity, not hostility.

The questions that follow are nearly always the same three: not even water? (no, not even water), the whole month? (daylight hours, every day), isn’t that dangerous? (hundreds of millions of people do it every year, and the sick, pregnant and travelling are exempt).

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What do I say at work or school?
English: If you are not out as a Muslim where you work or live, you do not have to be out to fast. A quiet “I’m not eating right now” has covered many first Ramadans, and the page on telling your family applies here too.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What if someone gives me a hard time?
English: What if someone gives me a hard time?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — What if someone gives me a hard time?
English: The instruction for exactly this moment is short: the fast is a shield, and if someone picks a fight or insults you while you are keeping it, you say “I am fasting” and leave it there. Out loud or under your breath — the point is that the fast changes how you answer provocation, not just what you eat.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Where are all the other Muslims, then?
English: Where are all the other Muslims, then?

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Where are all the other Muslims, then?
English:
At the mosque, every single evening. Ramadan is the one month a year when a mosque runs a free communal meal at sunset, open to whoever walks in — and when showing up alone is completely unremarkable, because half the room came alone. Nobody will ask why you are there. If anyone asks anything, it will be whether you have eaten.

If there is a month to make a mosque yours, it is this one. The night prayers afterwards are covered in the page on standing at night, and you can leave whenever you need to.

Where it appears: Fasting where nobody else is — Where are all the other Muslims, then?
English: Iftar time at the mosque follows the local sighting and the local minute, not this app’s calculation. When they differ, eat when the mosque eats.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Fasting in Ramadan
English: Fasting in Ramadan

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Fasting in Ramadan
English: No food, drink or intimacy from dawn until sunset, for the month of Ramadan.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Fasting in Ramadan
English: Ramadan moves through the year, so its length and difficulty change with the season. There are real exemptions for illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing, menstruation and old age, and taking one is not a failure. Some days are made up later, some are not.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Obligatory charity
English: Obligatory charity

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Obligatory charity
English: A yearly share of the wealth you have held onto, given to those entitled to it.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Obligatory charity
English: Zakat is not a donation you choose to make. It is a portion of your savings that stops being yours. It applies only above a threshold, and only to wealth you have held for a full lunar year, so many people newly earning owe none at all. The app can work out the sum for cash, gold and silver — but it counts nothing else, and whether it applies to you is still worth asking someone locally.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Pilgrimage
English: Pilgrimage

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Pilgrimage
English: The pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime, for those able to make it.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Pilgrimage
English: Hajj happens on fixed days of the Islamic year and is required once, and only if you can afford it and are physically able. Most Muslims go later in life, if at all. Nothing about it is expected of you now.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Prayer
English: Prayer

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Prayer
English: Five prayers a day, at set times, facing the Kaʿbah in Mecca.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Prayer
English: Fajr before sunrise, Dhuhr after midday, ʿAsr in the afternoon, Maghrib just after sunset, and ʿIshaʾ at night. Each one takes a few minutes. You wash first, which is wudu, and the app walks you through both.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — The testimony of faith
English: The testimony of faith

Where it appears: Five Pillars — The testimony of faith
English: Saying, and meaning, that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — The testimony of faith
English: This is the pillar the other four rest on. Saying it sincerely is what makes a person Muslim, and it is repeated in every prayer for the rest of your life. It is two statements held together: that worship belongs to Allah alone, and that Muhammad ﷺ is the one who conveyed how.

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: Is supermarket meat halal?

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: People genuinely differ, and you will be told opposite things with equal confidence. The Qur’an permits the food of the People of the Book; what scholars disagree about is whether modern industrial slaughter still resembles what that verse describes. Certified halal meat satisfies every position, which is where most converts start.

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: Muslims in Western countries genuinely differ on supermarket meat, and you will be told opposite things with equal confidence.

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: The starting point is not in dispute. All four schools hold that meat slaughtered by Jews and Christians is lawful, and all four hold that an animal killed by strangling, electrocution or anything other than cutting the throat was not lawfully slaughtered at all. What people disagree about is whether a modern slaughterhouse still meets that second condition. Stunning, mechanical blades and who is actually doing the slaughtering are all part of it. That makes it a question about how agreed rules apply today rather than a split between the schools, which is why this note names no school and counts nobody: some scholars hold the verse still covers ordinary supermarket meat, and others hold that industrial slaughter no longer resembles what it describes and restrict meat to what is certified. Buying certified halal meat satisfies every position, which is why most converts start there and settle the question later. Nobody is doing anything strange by taking the cautious route while they learn, and nobody is being lax by relying on the verse. The specifics are worth asking someone locally about rather than resolving from an article.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What about eating with my family?
English: What about eating with my family?

Where it appears: Food and drink — What about eating with my family?
English: You do not have to stop eating with people who are not Muslim, and you do not have to make a scene. Eat what you can, quietly leave what you cannot, and answer questions if they come. Most families adjust faster when the change is undramatic.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What about eating with my family?
English: Utensils that touched pork, or a shared roasting tin, worry converts far more than they worry most scholars. Wash it and move on.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What changes at the supermarket?
English: What changes at the supermarket?

Where it appears: Food and drink — What changes at the supermarket?
English: Reading labels, for a few weeks. Then it is automatic.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What is actually forbidden?
English: What is actually forbidden?

Where it appears: Food and drink — What is actually forbidden?
English: Four things, and the Qur’an names them outright.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Can I talk during the talk?
English: Can I talk during the talk?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Can I talk during the talk?
English: No, and this is the part visitors most often get wrong. The khuṭbah is listened to in silence — not whispered over, not scrolled through. The Prophet ﷺ said that even telling the person beside you to be quiet, while the imam is speaking, is itself idle talk. If somebody asks you something, a shake of the head is the answer.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Can I talk during the talk?
English: Phones on silent before you sit down, not after it starts. Everyone will hear you fumbling for it.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Do I have to go?
English: Do I have to go?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Do I have to go?
English: For men who can get there, yes — it is obligatory, not recommended, and that is the one thing about Friday worth being clear on. Women may attend and are welcome; it is not required of them, and a woman who prays Ḏuhr at home on a Friday has done what is asked.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Do I have to go?
English: That Jumuʿah is not obligatory on women is agreed across the schools. Attending is not discouraged — plenty of mosques have a full women’s section on a Friday.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Is this an extra prayer?
English: Is this an extra prayer?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — Is this an extra prayer?
English:
No. On Friday, the midday prayer is done differently: instead of praying Ḏuhr on your own, you go to a mosque, listen to a talk, and pray two rakʿah behind the imam. That is the whole of it, and it takes the place of Ḏuhr rather than being added to it.

If you pray Jumuʿah you do not then pray Ḏuhr. People new to this often do both, which is not required of them.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What actually happens?
English: What actually happens?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What actually happens?
English: You arrive, take your shoes off, and pray two short rakʿah on your own before sitting down. Then the imam gives a talk from the front — usually twenty minutes, in two parts with a short sit in between. When it ends, everyone stands and prays two rakʿah together. Then it is over and people leave.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if I arrive while it is happening?
English: What if I arrive while it is happening?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if I arrive while it is happening?
English:
Come in quietly and sit down where there is room. If you arrive during the talk, do not walk through the rows to find a better spot — and you still pray the two short rakʿah first, briefly, because the Prophet ﷺ told a man who came in during the khuṭbah to stand and pray them.

If you arrive after the congregation has already started praying, join the line where you are and follow the imam from wherever he has got to. When he finishes and gives salām, do not leave: stand back up and pray the rakʿahs you missed on your own. That last part is what completes your prayer.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if I arrive while it is happening?
English: Nobody minds a latecomer. Walking across the front of a room mid-talk is the only thing that draws a look.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if it is my first time?
English: What if it is my first time?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if it is my first time?
English: Then stand at the back, watch, and copy. Nobody is examining you, and every person in that room was new to it once. You do not have to speak to anyone, you do not have to introduce yourself, and you can leave straight afterwards.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — What if it is my first time?
English: If you would rather see the room before a Friday, go on a quieter day first. The mosque page covers that.

Where it appears: Friday prayer — When should I get there?
English: When should I get there?

Where it appears: Friday prayer — When should I get there?
English: Before the talk begins, which usually means ten or fifteen minutes before the advertised time. Coming early is encouraged in its own right, and it also spares you walking in front of a seated room. Washing and putting on clean clothes before you go is part of the day.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Intend
English: Intend in your heart that you are washing to lift the state you are in, then say:

Where it appears: Ghusl — Perform wudu
English: Perform wudu

Where it appears: Ghusl — Perform wudu
English: Do a complete wudu as you normally would, including rinsing your mouth and nose. You may leave washing your feet until the very end.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Pour over your head
English: Pour over your head

Where it appears: Ghusl — Pour over your head
English: Pour water over your head three times, working it through your hair until the water reaches the roots and the scalp is wet everywhere.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Pour over your head
English: Long hair does not need undoing for this, but the water has to reach the scalp underneath.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash the rest of you
English: Wash the rest of you

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash the rest of you
English: Pour water over the right side of your body, then the left, until every part of you has been reached: under the arms, behind the ears, between the toes. Nothing may be left dry.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash the rest of you
English: Take off anything water cannot pass, such as a ring or a watch, or move it as you go.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash your feet
English: If you left your feet until now, wash them, and you are finished.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash your feet
English: This ghusl counts as your wudu too. You can pray without repeating it, as long as nothing breaks your wudu afterwards.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash your hands
English: Wash both hands up to the wrists, three times.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash yourself
English: Wash yourself

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash yourself
English: Wash the private parts and anywhere else on the body carrying impurity, using your left hand. Then wash your hands again.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: When you need it

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Ghusl is required after sex, whether or not anything was released, and after any release of semen, including in your sleep. It is required when a period ends, and when bleeding after childbirth ends. Until you have done it, wudu is not enough and prayer is not valid.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: It is also recommended, though not required, before Friday prayer, before the two Eids, and for someone who has just become Muslim.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The thinner, clear fluid that comes with arousal is not the same thing and does not need a ghusl. Wash the part and the clothing it touched, do wudu, and pray.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: `Ali was too shy to ask and sent al-Miqdad to ask for him; the answer was that it requires wudu. This app said "any release of sexual fluid" before, which swept the two together and would have sent people for a full wash they did not owe. The books keep them apart carefully, and so does this.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Whether the wash on becoming Muslim is required or strongly recommended is a point scholars differ on. Doing it settles the question either way, which is why this app simply says to do it.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Two reports carry it. Thumamah ibn Uthal, released from the pillar of the mosque, went to a nearby grove, washed, came back and said the shahada. Bukhari files that under a chapter headed "taking a bath on embracing Islam". And Qays ibn `Asim came intending to accept Islam and was told to wash. Scholars read the second differently: some as a command, some as guidance. The recommended reading is the more common one, and it is not only held outside the Hanbali school: a group of Hanbalis report it from Ahmad himself, and al-Mardawi, whose job in that school was to say which position it settles on, chose it. What nobody holds is that your Islam is incomplete without it, and nobody thinks less of you for doing it a week later than the day itself.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The well-known position of the school holds the full wash obligatory on entering Islam.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Hold it recommended, unless something else, such as intimacy beforehand, had already made a ghusl due.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Hold it recommended rather than owed.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The Friday wash is strongly encouraged rather than owed, and all four schools treat it as a sunnah. The narration that settles it says a wudu on Friday is fine and good, and a ghusl is better.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: This used to be filed here as a difference between "the majority" and "a minority", which was vaguer than the evidence needs. All four schools hold the Friday ghusl a sunnah; the obligatory reading of Bukhari 877, "anyone of you attending the Friday prayer should take a bath", is held outside them. Tirmidhi records ash-Shafi`i's own argument for the first reading: `Umar was addressing the congregation when `Uthman arrived having only done wudu, and `Umar reproached him without sending him back to wash. Neither of them treated it as a condition, and both knew the instruction. One practical point the schools also agree on: it only counts as the Friday wash if it is done before the prayer.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The Eid wash is a companion's practice more than a narrated command. Ibn `Umar washed on the morning of Eid al-Fitr before setting out, and the practice has been kept ever since.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The narration that says the Prophet ﷺ himself washed on both Eids is graded weak by Darussalam, so it is not what the recommendation rests on and it is labelled here rather than quietly promoted. What it rests on is Malik's report of Ibn `Umar in the Muwatta. The hadith immediately after the weak one, Ibn Majah 1316, is graded fabricated. The app does not use it and never has.
