Where it appears: Halal and haram — Do I need permission for ordinary things?
English: Do I need permission for ordinary things?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — Do I need permission for ordinary things?
English: This is the part people get backwards. Things are permitted unless there is a clear reason otherwise, and the Qur’an describes the Prophet’s ﷺ message as making good things lawful rather than piling on prohibitions. You do not need to find permission for ordinary life.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What about things in between?
English: What about things in between?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What about things in between?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are matters that are unclear, which many people do not know about. Someone who stays away from what is doubtful protects their faith and their honour. That middle ground is where most real questions live.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What about things in between?
English: This is guidance for your own choices, not a licence to police anyone else’s. Being cautious about a doubtful thing for yourself is careful; declaring it forbidden for other people is a different act entirely.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What do halal and haram mean?
English: What do halal and haram mean?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What do halal and haram mean?
English: Halal means permitted. Haram means forbidden. They apply to everything, not just food: how you earn money, how you speak about people, what you wear. Most of life is halal and always was; the forbidden list is short.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What if I am not sure?
English: What if I am not sure?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What if I am not sure?
English: Ask someone qualified, and ask about your actual situation rather than the general case, because circumstances change answers. You will also meet Muslims who are certain of opposite answers on the same question. That usually means it is a genuine point of scholarly difference rather than that one of them is lying to you.

Where it appears: How prayer works — How do I actually learn it?
English: How do I actually learn it?

Where it appears: How prayer works — How do I actually learn it?
English:
By praying, with the guide open. Pick the next prayer of the day, follow it step by step on the mat, and let the pattern teach itself — after a week the guide is confirming what your body already knows. Nobody learns the prayer from a page and then performs it; everybody learns it by doing it imperfectly first.

And on a night when even that feels like too much, the least you can do is enough — that is its own page, and it is short.

Where it appears: How prayer works — So what changes between the five?
English: So what changes between the five?

Where it appears: How prayer works — So what changes between the five?
English: Only the count, and whether you hear the recitation:

Where it appears: How prayer works — So what changes between the five?
English: The Every prayer screen keeps this table one tap away, with the sunnah prayers that ride before and after each — you never need to hold it in memory.

Where it appears: How prayer works — What holds the rounds together?
English: What holds the rounds together?

Where it appears: How prayer works — What holds the rounds together?
English: Three joints, and the guides walk you through each: the prayer opens by saying Allāhu akbar; partway through — after the second rakʿah, in prayers longer than two — you sit briefly for the tashahhud; and at the very end you sit again, say the tashahhud, and close by turning your head to each side with the salam. Everything else is the rounds themselves.

Where it appears: How prayer works — What is one rakʿah?
English: What is one rakʿah?

Where it appears: How prayer works — What is one rakʿah?
English: A rakʿah is one round of the prayer’s movements. When the Prophet ﷺ was asked to teach the prayer, what he listed is short, and it is this round:

Where it appears: How prayer works — What is one rakʿah?
English: That is the unit. A four-rakʿah prayer is this, four times — nothing new appears in round three that was not in round one.

Where it appears: How prayer works — Why do the five prayers look identical?
English: Why do the five prayers look identical?

Where it appears: How prayer works — Why do the five prayers look identical?
English:
Because they are. Every prayer in Islam is the same movements and the same words, repeated a set number of times. Fajr is not one skill and Maghrib another — there is ONE skill, and it is smaller than the step-by-step guides make it look. Learn it once and you have learned every prayer you will ever pray, including the voluntary ones.

What changes from prayer to prayer is two facts: how many times round, and whether the Qur’an is recited aloud or quietly. That is the whole difference.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — How do I tell them?
English: How do I tell them?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — How do I tell them?
English:
Earlier than feels comfortable and more plainly than you want to. The thing that damages a relationship here is rarely the conversion; it is the six weeks of a partner sensing something has changed and not being told what.

You do not have to have all the answers before you talk to them. "This is real for me, I am still working out what it means, and I am not going anywhere" is a complete opening.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — How do I tell them?
English: A partner’s first reaction is often not their settled one. Give the conversation more than one attempt before concluding anything from it.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — Is my situation unusual?
English: Is my situation unusual?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — Is my situation unusual?
English:
No. Most people do not arrive at Islam alone — they arrive with a partner, or a marriage, or children, and often with none of it discussed yet. It is one of the most common convert situations there is, and any imam you speak to will have handled it many times before you.

What is uncommon is having anybody explain that in advance, which is why this page exists.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What happens to my marriage?
English: What happens to my marriage?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What happens to my marriage?
English:
It depends on who you both are, and the answer is genuinely not the same for everyone — which is precisely why this page will not give you one. What is worth knowing is that "you must divorce" is not the automatic answer people often assume, and that whoever tells you it is, without asking anything about your situation, is not the person to be advising you.

Take it to somebody who will ask questions first: your local imam, or a scholar you can actually speak to.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What happens to my marriage?
English: This is a genuine area of scholarly difference and of case-by-case ruling, not a settled single answer. Somebody who gives you one in a sentence has not understood the question.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What if we are together but not married?
English: What if we are together but not married?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What if we are together but not married?
English:
Then the shape you are being pointed towards is marriage, and the honest thing is that it will be a conversation rather than an announcement. Some people marry. Some separate. Some spend a long time somewhere in between while a partner works out what they think.

All three happen, and none of them means you failed at becoming Muslim.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What should I do first?
English: What should I do first?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — What should I do first?
English:
Nothing irreversible, and not today. If you have taken one thing from this page, take that.

People in exactly your position end marriages, leave homes and tell partners things they cannot take back, on the strength of a forum post or one confident acquaintance — and then find out the actual answer was different. There is no deadline on this. Pray tonight, and let this take the weeks it takes.

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — Who do I actually ask?
English: Who do I actually ask?

Where it appears: If you already have a partner — Who do I actually ask?
English:
A local imam, in person, with the specifics. Not a forum, not a group chat, and not the most confident person at the mosque — this is the kind of question where confidence and knowledge come apart, and where a wrong answer costs a marriage.

If approaching a mosque feels like too much, many have a person whose job is exactly this, and asking at the office rather than after prayer is entirely normal.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Am I still Muslim?
English: Am I still Muslim?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Am I still Muslim?
English:
Yes. Missing prayers — for a week, for a month, for longer — does not undo your shahada, and you do not say it again to come back. There is no re-entry, no ceremony, and nobody to tell.

That is worth reading twice, because the belief that you have to start again is the single most common reason people do not.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Do I have to tell anyone?
English: Do I have to tell anyone?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Do I have to tell anyone?
English: No. Not a friend, not an imam, not a group chat. There is no confession in Islam and nothing here needs a witness. If you want to tell somebody because carrying it alone is heavy, that is a good reason — but it is your reason, not a requirement.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — How do I actually come back?
English: How do I actually come back?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — How do I actually come back?
English: You pray the next prayer. That is the whole procedure. Not a plan, not a fresh start on Monday, not catching up on everything first — the next one, whenever it is, even if it is in twenty minutes and you do it badly.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — How do I actually come back?
English: If the full prayer feels like too much tonight, this app has a page on the least you can do. Use it. A short prayer tonight beats a perfect one you keep postponing.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What about all the prayers I missed?
English: What about all the prayers I missed?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What about all the prayers I missed?
English: They are a separate question from whether you are back, and they are not a debt you have to clear before you are allowed to start. Deal with the next prayer first. The app has a page on missed prayers for when you want to think about the rest, and it will keep.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What about all the prayers I missed?
English: Anybody who tells you to count up months of missed prayers before praying tonight has the order backwards.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What if it happens again?
English: What if it happens again?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What if it happens again?
English: Then you come back again, the same way, and it counts the same. Nothing about this gets used up, and the door does not close a second time any more than it did the first.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — What if it happens again?
English: People often relapse in a pattern — the same month, the same trigger. Noticing yours is more useful than promising it will not happen.

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Why does it feel so much worse than it is?
English: Why does it feel so much worse than it is?

Where it appears: If you stopped for a while — Why does it feel so much worse than it is?
English:
Because a gap makes people feel like frauds, and feeling like a fraud is much heavier than missing a prayer. Converts get this especially hard: there is often nobody who knew you before, so the gap feels like evidence that the whole thing was a phase.

It is not evidence of anything. The Prophet ﷺ said that he himself sought forgiveness and turned back to God more than seventy times in a day. Turning back is not the exception in this religion. It is the normal condition of being a person in it.

Where it appears: Isha — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Isha.

Where it appears: Isha — Turn to your left
English: That is Isha complete.

Where it appears: Istikhara — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Istikhara.

Where it appears: Istikhara — Then ask
English: Then ask

Where it appears: Istikhara — Then ask
English: The prayer is finished. Still sitting, say the duʿa, and where it says “this matter”, name the thing you are deciding.

Where it appears: Istikhara — Then ask
English: That is Istikhara complete.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — I have lost count. What now?
English: I have lost count. What now?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — I have lost count. What now?
English: If you cannot remember whether you are on the second or third rakʿah, assume the smaller one, the number you are certain of, and carry on from there.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — I have lost count. What now?
English: Do not start the prayer again. Restarting is the common instinct and it is not the answer.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — It keeps happening. Is that bad?
English: It keeps happening. Is that bad?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — It keeps happening. Is that bad?
English: Everyone loses count, including people who have prayed all their lives. If the doubt keeps coming back in the same prayer, ignore it and finish. Chasing certainty is itself a distraction from the prayer.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What are the two extra prostrations?
English: What are the two extra prostrations?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What are the two extra prostrations?
English: Finish the prayer as normal. Before or after the final taslim, make two prostrations just as you do in the prayer itself, saying the takbir as you go down and as you come up, then give the taslim.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What are the two extra prostrations?
English: Schools differ on whether these come before or after the taslim. Either is taught by scholars; do it the way whoever taught you does it.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What else does that fix cover?
English: What else does that fix cover?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What else does that fix cover?
English: Those two prostrations also cover forgetting the first sitting, adding a movement by mistake, or saying something in the wrong place.

Where it appears: Maghrib — Does it have to be right at sunset?
English: Does it have to be right at sunset?

Where it appears: Maghrib — Does it have to be right at sunset?
English: Its window runs until ʿIsha, but it is the shortest window of the five — which is why Maghrib is the prayer most often prayed the moment it arrives.

Where it appears: Maghrib — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Maghrib.

Where it appears: Maghrib — Turn to your left
English: That is Maghrib complete.

Where it appears: Maghrib — What is Maghrib?
English: What is Maghrib?

Where it appears: Maghrib — What is Maghrib?
English: Three rakʿahs as the light goes — the only odd count of the five, and the first prayer said aloud since dawn.

Where it appears: Maghrib — What is prayed after it?
English: What is prayed after it?

Where it appears: Maghrib — What is prayed after it?
English: Two quiet rakʿahs, part of the twelve daily voluntary rakʿahs the Prophet ﷺ tied to a house built in Paradise.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — So how do people actually meet?
English: So how do people actually meet?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — So how do people actually meet?
English:
Openly, and with somebody else around. There is no dating in the sense of a private relationship that may or may not become something — the assumption is that you are talking because you are considering marriage, and that it is not conducted alone.

In practice that looks like meeting through family, through a mosque, or through an app made for it, and then meeting in public or with somebody present. This is the part converts most often get wrong, usually by accident and usually by carrying over what they already knew.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What am I meant to be looking for?
English: What am I meant to be looking for?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What am I meant to be looking for?
English: The Prophet ﷺ listed the four things people marry for — wealth, family standing, beauty and religion — and said to choose the religious one. That is not a demand for austerity; it is a ranking, and it is the only one of the four that survives everything else changing.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What are the pieces called?
English: What are the pieces called?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What are the pieces called?
English: Four words that will come up constantly, and are never explained to a newcomer.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What are the pieces called?
English: What a walī is for, and what happens when a convert woman has no Muslim family, is a real question the schools answer differently. It is one to take to somebody local rather than settle from a page.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What if I am already married?
English: What if I am already married?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What if I am already married?
English: Then this page is not your question. Becoming Muslim while married is common and it has its own answer, which depends on who your spouse is and what happens next — it is covered on its own page, and this one would give you the wrong shape entirely.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What if I am already married?
English: Do not act on anything about an existing marriage from general reading. It is the single most common place converts are given bad advice by well-meaning strangers.

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What is a Muslim marriage?
English: What is a Muslim marriage?

Where it appears: Marriage, in shape — What is a Muslim marriage?
English:
A contract, agreed in front of witnesses. Not a sacrament and not a religious mystery — an offer, an acceptance, a gift from the husband to the wife, and people present who heard it. It can happen in a living room in ten minutes.

Most of what you will see at a wedding — the venue, the clothes, the several hundred guests — is culture on top of that, and none of it is the marriage.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — I missed a prayer. Is that a sin?
English: I missed a prayer. Is that a sin?

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — I missed a prayer. Is that a sin?
English: Sleeping through a prayer or forgetting it is not a sin. You pray it as soon as you wake or remember, and that prayer counts as the one you missed.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if I missed several?
English: What if I missed several?

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if I missed several?
English: Missed more than one? Pray them in the order they were due, then the prayer you are currently in time for.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if it keeps happening?
English: What if it keeps happening?

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if it keeps happening?
English: The thing that ends people’s prayer is not the prayer they missed. It is deciding they are now the sort of person who misses prayers. Pray the next one. That is the whole recovery.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if it keeps happening?
English: Deliberately leaving a prayer is a serious matter and different from oversleeping. The action is still the same: pray it, and pray the next one.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — Is everything I read a rule?
English: Is everything I read a rule?

Where it appears: Must, should, may — Is everything I read a rule?
English:
Read anything about Islam for a week and you will meet dozens of sentences that sound like instructions. Almost none of them are the same KIND of instruction, and if you read them all as commands you will end the month exhausted and convinced you are failing at everything.

There are five categories. Learning them once is the difference between a religion with a shape and a religion that is one long list.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What are the five?
English: What are the five?

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What are the five?
English: From the strongest to the strongest against, with everything ordinary in the middle.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What does it mean when this app says “should”?
English: What does it mean when this app says “should”?

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What does it mean when this app says “should”?
English: It usually means mustaḥabb — worth doing, not required. Where something is genuinely obligatory the app says so plainly, and where the schools of thought differ it says that too. You are not expected to hold all of it at once, and nothing here is keeping score.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What does it mean when this app says “should”?
English: Take the obligatory things first and let the rest arrive slowly. That is the order everybody learns them in.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What if nobody has told me either way?
English: What if nobody has told me either way?

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What if nobody has told me either way?
English: The starting position is that a thing is permitted unless there is a reason it is not. That is why the forbidden list is short and nameable, and why nobody can hand you a new prohibition without showing you where it comes from.

Where it appears: Must, should, may — What if nobody has told me either way?
English: A useful question when somebody tells you something is haram: which of the five, and on what basis? It is a fair question and it is not rude.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Does patience mean doing nothing?
English: Does patience mean doing nothing?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Does patience mean doing nothing?
English: Sabr means holding steady: carrying on doing the right thing while something is hard, rather than accepting whatever happens. The Qur’an pairs it with prayer as the two things to seek help through, which is a practical instruction more than a moral one: when it is bad, pray.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does gratitude actually mean?
English: What does gratitude actually mean?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does gratitude actually mean?
English: The Qur’an says that if you are grateful, He will increase you. Much of gratitude in practice is simply naming things, which is why al-ḥamdu li-llāh is said constantly, over small things, out loud. It is a habit of attention rather than a feeling you wait for.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does this look like for me now?
English: The first year often costs something real: family who do not understand, friends who drift, a life that has to be rearranged. That difficulty is not a sign you chose wrongly, and it is exactly the situation the word sabr is for.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Why are these always paired?
English: Why are these always paired?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Why are these always paired?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said the believer’s situation is remarkable, because everything that happens to them is good: when something pleasant comes they are grateful and that is good for them, and when something painful comes they are patient and that is good for them. Nobody else, he said, is in that position.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Do I still pray?
English: Do I still pray?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Do I still pray?
English: From the moment bleeding starts until it stops, you do not pray. This is not permission to skip. You are not supposed to pray, and praying anyway is not better.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Do I still pray?
English: You do not make these prayers up afterwards. They are not a debt. This surprises most people, so it is worth saying twice: they are simply not owed.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about after giving birth?
English: What about after giving birth?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about after giving birth?
English: Bleeding after childbirth follows the same rules as a period: you do not pray, you do not make those prayers up, and you take a ghusl when it ends.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about fasting?
English: What about fasting?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about fasting?
English: You do not fast during a period. Fasts missed in Ramadan for this reason are made up later, before the next Ramadan, at your own pace.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about fasting?
English: Prayer and fasting work differently here. Prayers are not made up; fasts are.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What can I still do?
English: What can I still do?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What can I still do?
English: Everything else stays open to you. You can make duʿa in your own words, say dhikr, listen to the Qur’an, go on learning, and sit with people who are praying.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What can I still do?
English: You are not unclean and you are not excluded. The rest from prayer is a concession you have been given, not a punishment or a mark against you.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What if the bleeding is not a period?
English: What if the bleeding is not a period?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What if the bleeding is not a period?
English: Bleeding outside your normal pattern, or lasting far beyond it, is treated differently, and it does not stop you praying. A woman asked the Prophet ﷺ exactly this and was told not to give up her prayers, because that bleeding comes from a blood vessel rather than being a period. You wash, do wudu, and pray; the wudu is done afresh for each prayer.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What if the bleeding is not a period?
English: Telling the two apart is genuinely a question for someone knowledgeable, not for an app. Do not guess, and do not stop praying on a guess.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — When do I start praying again?
English: When do I start praying again?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — When do I start praying again?
English: Once the bleeding has stopped, take a ghusl, the full wash, and you go straight back to praying with the next prayer due.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: Why do people tell me different things?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: One question here is genuinely open and two are not, and it saves a lot of confusion to know which is which. Reciting the Qur’an during a period is the open one: scholars divide on it, and you will meet people certain of opposite answers. Holding a printed muṣḥaf is not open in the same way, because all four schools say not to. Nor is sitting in the prayer hall of a mosque, which all four treat as somewhere not to stay through a period, though several allow walking through.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: None of this touches what the last section said. Listening, duʿa, dhikr and learning are open on every account, and nobody who tells you one of these is being difficult with you.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: On reciting the Qur’an there is no settled answer, and both sides are held by people who know exactly what they are doing.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: This section used to say scholars differ on all three of these and give no positions, which put a question all four schools agree on next to one they genuinely split over. On the muṣḥaf the agreement is about touching it; scholars treat a barrier between hand and page differently, so if you need to carry one or turn its pages, that is the thing to ask about. On the mosque the agreement is about remaining there. The Shafi`i and Hanbali schools permit passing through, and several contemporary scholars go further. If any of it affects your week, ask someone knowledgeable which position your local mosque follows.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: Permit reciting during a period, which is also al-Shafi`i’s earlier position and one narration from Ahmad.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: The settled positions of the Hanafi, Shafi`i and Hanbali schools hold back from reciting until the period ends.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn `Uthaymin took the permitting view, and it is the verdict of the Permanent Committee.

Where it appears: Phrase: Akhī · Ukhtī
English: My brother · my sister.

Where it appears: Phrase: Akhī · Ukhtī
English: How people will address you, including people who have just met you. It is ordinary, not familiar.

Where it appears: Phrase: Al-ḥamdu li-llāh
English: All praise is for Allah.

Where it appears: Phrase: Al-ḥamdu li-llāh
English: After good news, after eating, after sneezing, and as the normal answer to “how are you?”

Where it appears: Phrase: As-salāmu ʿalaykum
English: Peace be upon you.

Where it appears: Phrase: As-salāmu ʿalaykum
English: The greeting, arriving or passing. Said to you before almost anything else.

Where it appears: Phrase: As-salāmu ʿalaykum
English: Wa ʿalaykumu s-salām, and peace be upon you. Always answer it.

Where it appears: Phrase: Astaghfiru-llāh
English: I seek Allah’s forgiveness.

Where it appears: Phrase: Astaghfiru-llāh
English: Said after a slip, or on hearing something that should not have been said.

Where it appears: Phrase: Bāraka-llāhu fīk
English: May Allah bless you.

Where it appears: Phrase: Bāraka-llāhu fīk
English: Thanks, praise, or simply warmth towards you.

Where it appears: Phrase: Bāraka-llāhu fīk
English: Wa fīka bāraka-llāh, and may He bless you.

Where it appears: Phrase: In shāʾa-llāh
English: If Allah wills.

Where it appears: Phrase: In shāʾa-llāh
English: Attached to anything about the future. Not a soft no, whatever you may have been told. It is an acknowledgement that the future is not ours to promise.

Where it appears: Phrase: Innā li-llāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn
English: To Allah we belong, and to Him we return.

Where it appears: Phrase: Innā li-llāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn
English: On hearing that someone has died, or of a serious loss.

Where it appears: Phrase: Jazāka-llāhu khayran
English: May Allah reward you with good.

Where it appears: Phrase: Jazāka-llāhu khayran
English: Thank you. You will hear this far more often than the Arabic for “thanks”.

Where it appears: Phrase: Jazāka-llāhu khayran
English: Wa iyyāk, and you.

Where it appears: Phrase: Mā shāʾa-llāh
English: What Allah has willed.

Where it appears: Phrase: Mā shāʾa-llāh
English: Admiring something: a child, a new job, good news. Said so that admiration carries no envy with it.

Where it appears: Phrase: Raḍiya-llāhu ʿanhu
English: May Allah be pleased with him.

Where it appears: Phrase: Raḍiya-llāhu ʿanhu
English: Said after the name of one of the Prophet’s companions. “ʿanhā” for a woman.

Where it appears: Phrase: Ṣalla-llāhu ʿalayhi wa sallam
English: May Allah’s prayers and peace be upon him.

Where it appears: Phrase: Ṣalla-llāhu ʿalayhi wa sallam
English: Said after the Prophet’s name. Written as ﷺ, and that single character is this whole phrase.

Where it appears: Phrase: Subḥāna-llāh
English: Glory be to Allah.

Where it appears: Phrase: Subḥāna-llāh
English: Astonishment, at something beautiful or something terrible.

Where it appears: Phrase: Taqabbala-llāhu minnā wa minkum
English: May Allah accept it from us and from you.

Where it appears: Phrase: Taqabbala-llāhu minnā wa minkum
English: Around Eid and after Ramadan, about the worship of the month just gone.

Where it appears: Phrase: ʿĪd Mubārak
English: A blessed Eid.

Where it appears: Phrase: ʿĪd Mubārak
English: On either of the two Eids.

Where it appears: Phrase: ʿĪd Mubārak
English: Say it back.

Where it appears: Praying at night — How do I actually start?
English: How do I actually start?

Where it appears: Praying at night — How do I actually start?
English: Set an alarm twenty minutes before Fajr rather than for the middle of the night. You are already going to be awake for Fajr; this is standing up a little earlier. Starting there is why people keep it.

Where it appears: Praying at night — How little counts?
English: How little counts?

Where it appears: Praying at night — How little counts?
English: There is no minimum to reach and no number to work up to. Two rakʿahs, on one night, is the thing itself. People who pray it for decades mostly pray a little, often, which is the pattern the Prophet ﷺ described as the deeds God loves most, the small ones kept up.

Where it appears: Praying at night — How little counts?
English: It is the same prayer you already know. Nothing about the movements or the words changes. Only the time, and that you chose to be there.

Where it appears: Praying at night — What if I have not slept?
English: What if I have not slept?

Where it appears: Praying at night — What if I have not slept?
English: Tahajjud is prayed after waking, which is what separates it from simply staying up late. If you have not slept, you are praying qiyam al-layl, which is also good, also voluntary, and not what this word means.

Where it appears: Praying at night — What is tahajjud?
English: What is tahajjud?

Where it appears: Praying at night — What is tahajjud?
English: A prayer in the last part of the night, after you have slept and before Fajr. The Qur’an tells the Prophet ﷺ to keep part of the night for it as something additional, and that word matters: it is not owed. Nobody is behind for not praying it.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Do I still recite?
English: Do I still recite?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Do I still recite?
English: In the prayers said aloud — Fajr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ — the imam recites and you listen. In the silent ones you recite quietly to yourself as usual. Either way you say the same things in bowing and prostration that you would alone.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Do I still recite?
English: Whether you also read Al-Fātiḥah quietly behind the imam in an aloud prayer is a place the schools genuinely part company. Follow what the mosque you are in does, and nobody will think anything of it.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What am I actually meant to do?
English: What am I actually meant to do?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What am I actually meant to do?
English:
Follow him, and follow him slightly late. The Prophet ﷺ said the imam is appointed to be followed — so you bow when he has bowed, not with him and never before him. If you find yourself moving at the same moment, you are going too early.

That is most of it. The prayer is the same prayer you already know; what changes is that somebody else decides when.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I join late?
English: What if I join late?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I join late?
English: Join wherever they are, in the row where there is space, and follow from there. When the imam gives salām, stand back up and pray the rakʿahs you missed on your own. That last part is what completes your prayer, and it is the part people forget.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I lose track?
English: What if I lose track?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I lose track?
English: Keep following. You do not have to know which rakʿah it is — the imam does, and your job is to be in the same position he is. If everyone sits and you were about to stand, sit. Nobody is counting on your behalf and nobody is watching you the way it feels.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — What if I lose track?
English: If the imam makes a mistake, men say **subḥān Allāh** and women clap once. You will hear it happen; it is normal and it is not a scandal.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Where do I stand?
English: Where do I stand?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Where do I stand?
English: In the row, shoulder to shoulder, filling the gaps. Rows are straightened deliberately before the prayer starts and somebody may touch your shoulder or foot to line you up — that is not a correction of you, it is what happens to everyone. If a row is full, start the next one behind it.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Where do I stand?
English: Do not stand alone behind a full row if there is space in it. Step in; people will make room.

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Will anyone notice I am new?
English: Will anyone notice I am new?

Where it appears: Praying behind an imam — Will anyone notice I am new?
English: Less than you think. A room in prayer is looking forward, not sideways. Stand at the back, copy the person next to you, and accept that you will be half a second behind everything — which is, technically, exactly right.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — Does it count the same?
English: Does it count the same?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — Does it count the same?
English: A prayer prayed sitting because you could not stand is not worth less than one prayed standing. It is the prayer you were asked for.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — How do I bow and prostrate?
English: How do I bow and prostrate?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — How do I bow and prostrate?
English: Lean forward a little for the bowing, and further forward for the prostration, so that the prostration is clearly lower than the bow. Say everything exactly as you would standing.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot sit either?
English: What if I cannot sit either?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot sit either?
English: Pray lying on your right side facing the qibla, or on your back, and make the movements with your head or your eyes. Prayer is never dropped for illness while you are conscious.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot stand?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — Can I pray two together?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: How far counts as travelling?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: Far enough that you would ordinarily call it travelling. There is no distance in the Qur’an or in any narration, so scholars have had to draw the line themselves, and they draw it in different places. The most common answer works out at somewhere around eighty to ninety kilometres. What everyone agrees on is when it starts: not when you decide to go, but once you have actually left the place you live.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: A daily commute is not a journey, however long it feels. If you are unsure, ask someone locally rather than deciding alone.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: No verse and no narration gives a distance. The figure most scholars use is a conversion of a classical measure, and a second position holds there is no fixed distance at all: if it is a journey, you may shorten.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: The app used to say "roughly eighty kilometres" without saying where the number came from, which made a scholarly conversion look like a reported figure. A barid is a classical measure of distance, and four of them is two days of loaded-camel travel; converted into modern units it lands near eighty-eight kilometres, and different conversions give slightly different numbers, which is most of why you will hear eighty from one person and ninety from another. How long you may keep shortening once you arrive is a second difference again. The Maliki and Shafi`i schools stop at four days, the Hanafi school at fifteen, and some hold there is no limit while you have not settled.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: The Maliki, Shafi`i and Hanbali schools put it at four burud, which converts to roughly eighty-eight kilometres.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: Reckon it from a journey of about three days at the pace people travelled then, which the school gives as forty-eight miles, or roughly seventy-seven kilometres.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn `Uthaymin held there is no fixed distance: anything ordinarily called travelling counts.

English: How much do I pray when travelling?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How much do I pray when travelling?
English: On a journey, the four-rakʿah prayers, Dhuhr, ʿAsr and ʿIshaʾ, are prayed as two. Fajr stays two and Maghrib stays three.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How much do I pray when travelling?
English: This is a gift, not a compromise. It is the practice of the Prophet ﷺ on journeys, not a lowering of the bar.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What are suhoor and iftar?
English: What are suhoor and iftar?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What are suhoor and iftar?
English: Suhoor is the meal before dawn. The Prophet ﷺ said to take it, because there is blessing in it, and skipping it makes a long day much harder. Iftar is breaking the fast at sunset, traditionally with dates and water, and he taught not to delay it once the sun is down.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What does the fast involve?
English: What does the fast involve?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What does the fast involve?
English: From first light until sunset, no food, no drink, not even water, and no sexual intimacy. The Qur’an marks the start of the fast as the moment dawn becomes distinguishable, and the end at sunset. Outside those hours you eat and drink normally.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: What happens at the end?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: The month ends with Eid: a morning prayer, new or good clothes, and visiting people. Before that prayer, every Muslim gives a small fixed amount of food so that nobody is left out of the day. It is called zakat al-fitr and it is due for every member of a household, old and young, and paid on behalf of anyone in your care.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Whether it may be given as money instead of food is a real difference, and it decides what you actually hand over. Most mosques and charities collect it either way and will tell you which they are doing.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Nothing about your Eid depends on getting this right in your first year. Give it through whoever your local mosque collects for, in the form they ask for, before the Eid prayer. That satisfies the position they follow, and the timing is the part the narration is strictest about.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Allow the value in money, and consider it easier for the recipient.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Malik, ash-Shafi`i and Ahmad hold that it is the staple food the narration names, given as food rather than as its value.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens the rest of the month?
English: What happens the rest of the month?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens the rest of the month?
English: Mosques fill up for taraweeh, a long optional night prayer, and many people read far more Qur’an than usual. Jibril would go through the Qur’an with the Prophet ﷺ each night of Ramadan. There is also more giving: he was described as at his most generous this month.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Laylat al-Qadr?
English: What is Laylat al-Qadr?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Laylat al-Qadr?
English: One night in Ramadan is called Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Decree, the night the Qur’an began to be revealed, which the Qur’an says is better than a thousand months. Nobody is told which night it is. The Prophet ﷺ said to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten, which is why mosques fill up at the end of the month.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Ramadan?
English: What is Ramadan?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Ramadan?
English: The ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, and the month in which the Qur’an began to be revealed. Because the calendar is lunar, it moves about eleven days earlier each year, so it passes through every season over a lifetime.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Who does not have to fast?

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: The Qur’an names two: anyone ill, and anyone travelling. Both make the days up afterwards, at their own pace, before the next Ramadan. It also gives a second route for someone who could only fast with real hardship: feeding a poor person for each day instead of fasting it. That second route is the answer for a long-term or permanent condition, where making the days up later is not something that is ever going to happen. During a period a woman does not fast either, and those days are made up.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: If you are on medication or managing an illness, ask a doctor and someone knowledgeable before your first Ramadan rather than during it. A first Ramadan is far more often damaged by someone fasting who should not have than by someone taking an exemption they were given.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Not fasting when you are exempt is not a failure and not something to feel guilty about. The exemption is part of the instruction, not a loophole in it.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Pregnancy and breastfeeding are the case scholars genuinely divide over. That you may stop fasting where there is real risk to you or the baby is agreed; what you owe afterwards is not, and the answer can turn on whether the worry was for you or for the child.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: This lesson used to say the exemptions were covered by "makes the days up later", which is one of these four answers stated as though it were the ruling. There is a fifth position that is older than all of them: Ibn `Abbas and Ibn `Umar held that a pregnant or breastfeeding woman feeds a poor person for each day and does not make the days up at all, which is the gentlest of the answers and is still taught. Among contemporary scholars, Ibn Baz, Ibn `Uthaymin and the Permanent Committee held that the days are made up. Nothing here needs deciding in the abstract: work out with someone knowledgeable what applies to your own situation, and do it before Ramadan rather than in the middle of it.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Make the days up, and nothing else is owed.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: A pregnant woman makes the days up. A breastfeeding woman makes them up and also feeds a poor person for each day.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: If she stopped fasting out of fear for herself, she makes the days up. If out of fear for the child alone, she makes them up and feeds a poor person for each day.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: The same distinction as the Shafi`i school.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Feeding a poor person for each missed day is what "fidyah" means when you hear the word. Most mosques and Muslim charities collect it and will tell you the amount they use locally.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Why fast at all?
English: Why fast at all?

Where it appears: Ramadan — Why fast at all?
English: The Qur’an gives the reason directly: so that you may become mindful of God. It is not endurance for its own sake, and it is not a diet. Being hungry at four in the afternoon is a reminder of who provides, and of people for whom that hunger is not a choice.

Where it appears: Standing at night — Where will I hear the word?
English: Where will I hear the word?

Where it appears: Standing at night — Where will I hear the word?
English: In Ramadan, mosques announce “qiyam” for the long night prayers in the last ten nights. Taraweeh is the same family of prayer. You are welcome at it, you can leave when you need to, and nobody is counting your rakʿahs.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Tahajjud.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — Turn to your left
English: That is Tahajjud complete.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Intend
English: Intend in your heart that you are purifying yourself for prayer, in place of using water.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Touch the ground
English: Touch the ground

Where it appears: Tayammum — Touch the ground
English: Place both palms flat on a clean natural surface: earth, sand, stone, or dust settled on something. Lift them and shake off any excess.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Touch the ground
English: It does not have to be soil. A dusty windowsill or a stone wall will do.

Where it appears: Tayammum — When it ends
English: When it ends

Where it appears: Tayammum — When it ends
English: Tayammum breaks for the same reasons wudu breaks, and it ends the moment water becomes available to you.

Where it appears: Tayammum — When you can use it
English: When you can use it

Where it appears: Tayammum — When you can use it
English: Tayammum replaces wudu, and replaces ghusl, when there is no water you can reach, when using it would make you ill or make an illness worse, or when the only water available is needed for drinking.

Where it appears: Tayammum — When you can use it
English: It is not for when water is merely inconvenient. But it is genuinely allowed when it applies, and people miss prayers they were permitted to pray.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your face
English: Wipe your face

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your face
English: Wipe both palms once over your whole face.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: Wipe your hands

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: Wipe the back of your right hand to the wrist with your left palm, then the back of your left hand with your right. You are finished and may pray.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: Some schools wipe the arms to the elbows instead of stopping at the wrists. Both are taught by scholars; you will see people do it either way.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: In the narration the Prophet ﷺ struck the earth once, blew the dust off, and wiped the face and the backs of the hands. The two wordings Bukhari carries put those in either order, which is why you will see both taught. This guide follows the order of the wudu verse: face, then hands. Schools that teach wiping to the elbows argue from other narrations and from that same verse. Nobody will think you have prayed invalidly either way.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Am I supposed to say something back?
English: Am I supposed to say something back?

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Am I supposed to say something back?
English: Quietly repeating what the caller says, line by line, is the ordinary thing to do while it is happening — and there is a short duʿa said afterwards. Neither is obligatory, and neither is complicated.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Am I supposed to say something back?
English: If you do not know the words yet, listening is enough. Nobody is watching, and nobody starts out knowing them.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Does this mean I am late?
English: Does this mean I am late?

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Does this mean I am late?
English: Hearing the adhān for a prayer you have not prayed does not mean you are late. It means that prayer has just become available. The times card on the Today screen shows when each window closes, which is the part worth knowing.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Does this mean I am late?
English: Mosques call at slightly different minutes from a calculated timetable. If your mosque differs from this app, follow the mosque.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — What am I hearing?
English: What am I hearing?

Where it appears: The call to prayer — What am I hearing?
English:
The adhān is the announcement that a prayer’s time has come in. It is called out — from a mosque, from a phone, sometimes by one person in a room — and it happens five times a day at the times in this app.

It is not a summons you are late for and it is not a countdown. It marks the opening of a window, and the window is usually hours long.

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Why did it happen twice?
English: Why did it happen twice?

Where it appears: The call to prayer — Why did it happen twice?
English: The adhān announces the time. A second, shorter call — the iqāmah — is given immediately before a congregation actually starts praying. If you are in a mosque and hear a second one a few minutes after the first, that is people standing up to pray, not a mistake.

Where it appears: The least you can do — Is a short prayer still a prayer?
English: Is a short prayer still a prayer?

Where it appears: The least you can do — Is a short prayer still a prayer?
English:
The guides in this app walk you through a prayer at its fullest — every position, every word, in order. That is what to aim at, and it is not the bar. A prayer done briefly, plainly, with the essentials in place, is a prayer. It is not half a prayer and it does not need making up later.

This page exists because reading "23 steps" on a night when you have four minutes and no confidence can make praying feel out of reach. It is not.

Where it appears: The least you can do — Is a short prayer still a prayer?
English: On a hard day, the least is the right amount. Nobody is grading the difference.

Where it appears: The least you can do — Is it better to rush it or pray it late?
English: Is it better to rush it or pray it late?

Where it appears: The least you can do — Is it better to rush it or pray it late?
English: The prayer has fixed times, and the time is part of it. Given the choice between a short prayer inside its window and a careful one after the window has closed, pray the short one. The full shape will come; the time will not come back.

Where it appears: The least you can do — What actually has to be there?
English: What actually has to be there?

Where it appears: The least you can do — What actually has to be there?
English: A man once prayed in the mosque and the Prophet ﷺ told him three times to go back and pray, because he had not prayed. The man asked to be taught, and what he was taught is the shortest description of a prayer there is.

Where it appears: The least you can do — What actually has to be there?
English: The word doing the work is "settle". Rushing is the one thing that narration corrects, and it corrects it three times.

Where it appears: The least you can do — What if I only know Al-Fatihah?
English: What if I only know Al-Fatihah?

Where it appears: The least you can do — What if I only know Al-Fatihah?
English: Then you have what you need. Al-Fatihah is the part the prayer does not do without, and anything after it is more rather than necessary. If you are still learning the words, read them from the screen — nobody has to hold them in memory before they are allowed to start.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: How does this affect my week?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: For most of the year, not at all — you will pick the date up from the people around you and never need to work it out. It only matters at the two ends of Ramadan, and there it is announced locally rather than calculated in advance, so mosques in the same city can start the month or the Eid a day apart. That is normal and not worth worrying about.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Whether a month begins by sighting the moon locally or by astronomical calculation is a live question, and communities in the same country sometimes start Ramadan on different days.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Both approaches are argued from evidence and neither community is being careless. As a beginner the practical answer is to follow the mosque or community you pray with. Scholars have discussed this in more detail.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Follow the sighting of the moon, as reported locally or regionally.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Some bodies accept astronomical calculation to fix the date in advance.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the sacred months?
English: What are the sacred months?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the sacred months?
English: The Qur’an says four of the twelve are sacred, and the Prophet ﷺ named them in his farewell sermon: three consecutive ones, Dhul-Qaʿdah, Dhul-Hijjah and Muharram, and Rajab. Fighting is prohibited in them, and wrongdoing in them is treated as more serious.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the twelve months?
English: What are the twelve months?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the twelve months?
English: In order, from the top of the year. Four are sacred, two carry an Eid and one carries the fast; the other five have nothing in them at all. Several are named for a season they no longer fall in — Rabiʿ is spring, Jumada is the dry part of the year — because the months kept moving and the names did not.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the twelve months?
English: You may hear that Safar is an unlucky month, or that it is a bad time to marry or travel. That is a pre-Islamic superstition, and the Prophet ﷺ named it and rejected it. No month carries bad luck.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Which months ask anything of me?
English: Which months ask anything of me?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Which months ask anything of me?
English: Only one thing in the year is obligatory, and it is Ramadan, which has a lesson of its own. Four others are worth knowing because you will hear all four mentioned and none of them is required: the fast of ʿAshuraʾ on the tenth of Muharram, which the Prophet ﷺ kept and which became voluntary once Ramadan was prescribed; fasting through Shaʿban, which he did more of than in any month but Ramadan; six fasts spread through Shawwal after Ramadan; and the first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah, which he described as the best days of the year for doing good.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Why does the date move every year?
English: Why does the date move every year?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Why does the date move every year?
English: Twelve months, each beginning with a new moon, making a year about eleven days shorter than the solar one. That is why Ramadan and the two Eids move earlier every year rather than falling on fixed dates. Over a lifetime they pass through every season.

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?
English: Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?
English: You are forgiven by turning back to God and meaning it. There is no ceremony and nothing to perform. This prayer is something you may do, not a step you have missed. It exists because doing something with your body often helps when saying it in your head does not.

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?
English: There is no limit, and no shame in praying it often. Somebody who prays it twice in a week has not failed twice. They have turned back twice.

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — What is it for?
English: What is it for?

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — What is it for?
English: Abu Bakr reported that the Prophet ﷺ said no one does something wrong, then gets up and purifies himself, then prays, then asks God’s forgiveness, except that God forgives him. Wudu, two rakʿahs, and asking. That is the whole of it.

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying The prayer of repentance.

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — Turn to your left
English: That is The prayer of repentance complete.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — How many should I take on?
English: How many should I take on?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — How many should I take on?
English:
One. Then, once it has stopped being something you remember to do, one more.

The way this goes wrong is a person adopting twelve at once in their first month, keeping none of them past week three, and concluding they are bad at being Muslim. Nothing here is a checklist and nothing is measured. A habit you have held for two years is worth more than eleven you dropped.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What about the little duʿas?
English: What about the little duʿas?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What about the little duʿas?
English: They are already in this app, in the duʿa book, with the book’s own wording: waking, leaving the house, entering and leaving the bathroom, before and after eating, entering a mosque. This page does not print them a second time — one text belongs in one place, and there it can be searched, pinned and read in Arabic and English together.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What about the little duʿas?
English: The duʿa tab has them grouped by moment. Take one, use it for a fortnight until you stop having to look, and only then take another.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What are they?
English: What are they?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What are they?
English:
Small habits the Prophet ﷺ kept, which Muslims take on gradually over years. Starting with the right side. Cleaning your teeth. A short duʿa on waking, on leaving the house, before eating. None of them is required, none is difficult, and together they turn ordinary parts of a day into something deliberate.

They are the part of the religion that is least discussed with converts and most visible in people who have been Muslim a long time.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What is the siwak?
English: What is the siwak?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — What is the siwak?
English:
A twig from the arāk tree, used to clean the teeth — you will see them sold outside mosques for very little. The Prophet ﷺ said that were it not hard on people, he would have ordered it before every prayer, which tells you both how much he valued it and that he did not make it a requirement.

A toothbrush achieves the cleaning. Many people use the siwak anyway, before prayer and on Fridays.

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — Why do people start with the right?
English: Why do people start with the right?

Where it appears: The small sunnahs — Why do people start with the right?
English:
Because he did. ʿĀʾishah described him as liking to begin with the right side — putting on shoes, combing his hair, washing. It applies to entering a room, eating, giving and taking. The left is used for the opposite: leaving a bathroom, removing shoes.

It is a small thing that becomes automatic within about a week, and it is the easiest of these to start with.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — Rejecting the truth — what does that mean in practice?
English: Rejecting the truth — what does that mean in practice?

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — Rejecting the truth — what does that mean in practice?
English: Knowing you are wrong and not saying so. It is the half of the definition people skip, because it does not feel like arrogance from the inside; it feels like holding your ground. But refusing a correction because of who gave it, or because taking it would be embarrassing, is the thing being named — and it is much more common than looking down on anybody.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What counts as arrogance?
English: What counts as arrogance?

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What counts as arrogance?
English: He ﷺ said that nobody with an atom’s weight of kibr in his heart enters Paradise. A man in the gathering heard that and asked the obvious question — a person likes his clothes to look good, and his shoes. He was told that Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, and then given the definition: kibr is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What counts as arrogance?
English: The answer is worth as much as the warning. Somebody heard a hard statement, applied it to himself in the wrong place, and was corrected on the spot. Arrogance is not self-respect, tidiness or confidence.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What does this look like for me now?
English: It arrives in two directions and the second one is the surprise. Someone will correct your prayer in a tone that has nothing to do with your prayer, and it will sting. But new certainty is its own risk: three months in, it is easy to look at the family you left, or at Muslims who seem casual about it, and quietly rank yourself. You have no idea what anybody else is carrying, and none of the people you are ranking know how long you will keep this up either.

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What is the opposite?
English: What is the opposite?

Where it appears: Thinking you are better — What is the opposite?
English: Not thinking badly of yourself. Humility here is a downward movement you make on purpose, and the promise attached to it runs the other way: charity does not decrease wealth, forgiving someone only increases a person’s honour, and no one humbles himself for Allah except that Allah raises him. All three are counter-intuitive on purpose — each names the thing you fear losing and says you will not lose it.

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — Is wanting what someone has always wrong?
English: Is wanting what someone has always wrong?

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — Is wanting what someone has always wrong?
English: No, and the distinction is exact. Do not wish to be like anyone, he ﷺ said, except in two cases: a man Allah gave wealth who spends it rightly, and a man Allah gave wisdom who acts by it and teaches it. Wanting the same good for yourself, with no wish that they lose theirs, is the permitted kind — Arabic calls it ghibṭah. Ḥasad proper is wanting the thing gone from them, and that is a complaint about who was given what, aimed past the person at the One who gave it.

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — What actually stops it?
English: What actually stops it?

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — What actually stops it?
English: A change of direction, given as a practical instruction rather than an attitude: when one of you looks at somebody given more than him in wealth or in looks, let him look at someone who has less. Envy is largely a matter of where the eye rests by default. The instruction does not ask you to feel differently. It asks you to look somewhere else, and lets the feeling follow.

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — What does this look like for me now?
English: The thing converts envy is not usually money. It is somebody reading Arabic without thinking about it, a family that eats together at iftar, twenty years of this already behind them, a name that fits. None of that is available to want — it is a childhood, and it is gone. What the permitted kind allows is the part that is still open: you can want the Arabic and go and get it, slowly, badly at first. The rest is worth grieving rather than resenting, and they are not the same thing.

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — Where does envy sit?
English: Where does envy sit?

Where it appears: Wanting what someone else has — Where does envy sit?
English: In a list, and the company it keeps is the point. Beware of suspicion, he ﷺ said, for suspicion is the falsest of speech; do not spy, do not envy one another, do not turn away from one another, do not hate one another — be servants of Allah, brothers. Every item is a way one person’s inner life quietly wrecks a group, and envy is filed with them rather than treated as a private feeling.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — Can I move at all?
English: Can I move at all?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — Can I move at all?
English: Scratching, shifting your weight, stepping forward to close a gap, picking up a child: none of this ends the prayer. What is meant by movement breaking it is a lot of it, continuously, for no reason connected to praying. The Prophet ﷺ prayed while carrying his granddaughter, putting her down to prostrate and picking her back up.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What about ordinary mistakes?
English: What about ordinary mistakes?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What about ordinary mistakes?
English: Losing count, forgetting a sitting, adding a movement, saying something in the wrong place: none of these break the prayer. They are fixed with two extra prostrations at the end, which the app covers separately. A beginner will do all of these, and none of them is a disaster.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What about ordinary mistakes?
English: The most common beginner mistake is starting the prayer over. Almost nothing requires that, and restarting turns a small slip into a long one.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: What actually breaks it?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: Losing your wudu. Speaking on purpose to someone. Eating or drinking. Laughing out loud. Turning your body right away from the qibla, or deciding to stop. If one of these happens, put it right and pray it again from the beginning. But read the rest of this page first, because almost every one of them has an exception, and most of what a beginner worries about is on the other list.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: Smiling is not laughing, and nobody has ever held that it breaks a prayer. What is meant is laughing aloud.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: Ibn al-Mundhir recorded the scholars as agreed that laughing aloud ends the prayer, and an-Nawawi and Ibn Qudamah both record that most of them held smiling does not. It is one of the few things on this page nobody argues about. One thing they do differ on is what else it costs you: the Maliki, Shafi`i and Hanbali schools hold that laughing aloud ends the prayer but leaves your wudu intact, so you stand up and pray again. The Hanafi school holds that it ends the wudu too, so someone following that school washes first. If you are not sure which applies to you, washing again costs a minute.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: What if I am facing the wrong way?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: This one is narrower than it sounds. What ends the prayer is turning your whole body away from the qibla with no reason to. Getting the direction wrong, in a hotel room or on a plane or in a city you do not know, does not, as long as you worked it out as best you could. If you find out afterwards that you were off, the prayer stands.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: A whole congregation once turned right around in the middle of Fajr, and their prayer counted.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: The people of Quba were praying facing Jerusalem when someone arrived to say the direction had been changed to the Ka`bah that night, so they turned mid-prayer and carried on. Bukhari puts the narration under a chapter heading that includes those who held there is no need to repeat a prayer offered by mistake in the wrong direction.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: What if I speak without thinking?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: A companion said "Allah have mercy on you" to a man who sneezed mid-prayer, not knowing he could not. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ taught him, without scolding him and by his own account better than anyone had ever taught him anything, that this prayer is not the place for ordinary speech. He was not told to pray it again. Deliberate speech ends the prayer; speech before you knew the rule, or in a moment of forgetfulness, does not.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: This was not always the rule. People used to speak to each other in prayer and were told to stop, which is why the narrations about it read the way they do.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: Zayd ibn Arqam: "we used to speak while praying, and one of us would tell his companion what he needed, until the verse was revealed and we were ordered to be silent." Ibn Mas`ud used to greet the Prophet ﷺ mid-prayer and be answered, and returned from Abyssinia to find that he was not: "there is occupation enough in the prayer".

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I think I broke wudu?
English: What if I think I broke wudu?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I think I broke wudu?
English: Doubt does not. Someone asked the Prophet ﷺ about feeling as though they had passed wind mid-prayer, and he said not to leave the prayer unless they heard a sound or smelled something. Uncertainty is not enough. Carry on.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I think I broke wudu?
English: This is the hadith to remember if you find yourself checking constantly. The rule is deliberately strict about certainty, because doubt would otherwise end every prayer.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Do I have to tell anyone what I did?
English: Do I have to tell anyone what I did?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Do I have to tell anyone what I did?
English: There is no confession in Islam. Nobody at a mosque needs your history, no imam has to hear it, and nothing about your becoming Muslim requires you to describe what you are leaving. Anyone who asks is asking for themselves, not for the religion, and you can decline.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Do I have to tell anyone what I did?
English: That includes online. You do not owe your story to a forum, a group chat, or anyone who says it will help others.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Does my past come with me?
English: Does my past come with me?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Does my past come with me?
English:
A companion of the Prophet ﷺ, near the end of his life, said that when Islam entered his heart he asked to give his pledge — and was told that Islam demolishes what came before it. Not forgives it slowly. Demolishes.

You did not arrive owing for those years. No debt carried over, no probation, nothing to work off.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Is it only cancelled?
English: Is it only cancelled?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Is it only cancelled?
English: The Qur’an goes further than clearing the account. For those who turn, believe and do right, it says the wrongs are exchanged for good — not merely wiped, but swapped. Read that once and then again, because it is not what most people expect a religion to say about their worst years.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — What about the things that have not gone away?
English: What about the things that have not gone away?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — What about the things that have not gone away?
English:
Some of the past is not past. A marriage, children, a job, money, family who do not know. Those are real and they do not vanish, and this page is not going to pretend otherwise or rule on them — they have conditions on them and they need somebody who knows your situation.

What has already been settled is the part underneath: none of it disqualifies you, and none of it has to be solved before you pray tonight.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — What about the things that have not gone away?
English: Take these one at a time and slowly. A convert given six life decisions in their first month usually makes them badly.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Why do I still feel guilty?
English: Why do I still feel guilty?

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Why do I still feel guilty?
English: It often does, and it is not a sign that something was left undone. The Qur’an tells people who have wronged themselves not to despair, and the address is to them specifically — not to people who have nothing to regret. Feeling it is not evidence against you.

Where it appears: What happens to the life before — Why do I still feel guilty?
English: If it becomes heavy rather than passing, that is worth telling a person you trust.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it belief, or practice?
English: Is it belief, or practice?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it belief, or practice?
English: When the angel Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ about this in front of his companions, the answer came in two parts: what you believe, and what you do. Neither stands alone. That is why this app teaches the prayer and the belief side by side rather than one first and one later.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it meant to be this hard?
English: Is it meant to be this hard?
