Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it meant to be this hard?
English: You are not behind. The Prophet ﷺ said the religion is easy, and that whoever overburdens themselves in it will not keep it up, so take the next thing rather than all of it. The Qur’an says God does not ask of anyone more than they can bear.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does it ask of me?
English: What does it ask of me?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does it ask of me?
English: The testimony of faith, the five daily prayers, zakat, a yearly share of savings given to those entitled to it, fasting in Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime for anyone able to make it. The Prophet ﷺ described Islam as built on these five.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does the word mean?
English: What does the word mean?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does the word mean?
English: Islam is an Arabic word meaning submission, giving yourself over to God. A Muslim is someone who does that. It comes from the same root as salam, peace, and the two ideas sit together: peace through no longer being pulled in every direction at once.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What is at the centre of it?
English: What is at the centre of it?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What is at the centre of it?
English: Everything else rests on this. Islam teaches that there is one God, Allah, the Arabic word for God used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews too, and that worship belongs to Him alone, with nothing and no one sharing it. Saying and meaning that is what makes a person Muslim.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What is at the centre of it?
English: Nobody can be forced into this. The Qur’an says plainly that there is no compulsion in religion.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Am I already reading it?
English: Am I already reading it?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Am I already reading it?
English: The Qur’an is not only read, it is recited, in every prayer, out loud or quietly. Al-Fatihah, its opening chapter of seven short verses, is said in every unit of every prayer for the rest of your life. Learning it is the single most useful thing a new Muslim can memorise.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Am I already reading it?
English: Until you know it, say what you can and keep learning. Nobody starts fluent, and the Practice screen exists to take it a line at a time.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — What do Muslims believe it is?
English: What do Muslims believe it is?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — What do Muslims believe it is?
English: Not a book about God, but the speech of God, revealed in Arabic to Muhammad ﷺ through the angel Jibril over about twenty-three years, and preserved unchanged since. That is the claim, and it is why the Arabic itself matters so much: a translation is understood as an explanation of the Qur’an rather than the Qur’an.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Where should I start?
English: Where should I start?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Where should I start?
English: Start small and start with sound. Learn Al-Fatihah, then a few of the short chapters at the end, listening and repeating rather than reading silently. The Prophet ﷺ said the best of people are those who learn the Qur’an and teach it. Learning it is the point, and it is slow for everyone.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Why does it not start at the beginning?
English: Why does it not start at the beginning?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Why does it not start at the beginning?
English: It has 114 chapters, called surahs, made of verses called ayahs. They are not in the order they were revealed, and it is not a story told front to back, so reading it cover to cover like a novel is not how most people start, and struggling with that is not a failure of yours.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Are all hadith reliable?
English: Are all hadith reliable?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Are all hadith reliable?
English: Because hadith were transmitted by people, scholars spent centuries grading them, examining every chain and every narrator. Some are sound, some are weak, and some are forgeries. This is why the app names its sources: so you can check, rather than take its word.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Are all hadith reliable?
English: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are the two collections Sunni scholars regard as the most rigorously authenticated. Other collections contain both strong and weak reports, which is why a grading matters there and not in these two.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does it look like day to day?
English: What does it look like day to day?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does it look like day to day?
English: Much of it is small and human: not harming a neighbour, making a guest welcome, saying something good or staying quiet, eating with the right hand, a few words before sleeping. Following the Sunnah is not an extra layer of difficulty on top of the religion. A lot of it is simply how a decent person moves through a day.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does Sunnah mean?
English: What does Sunnah mean?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does Sunnah mean?
English: Sunnah means a way or a path, and specifically the way the Prophet ﷺ lived: what he said, what he did, and what he approved of in others. It reaches us through hadith, which are reports of those things recorded with the chain of people who passed each one down.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Why does it sit beside the Qur’an?
English: Why does it sit beside the Qur’an?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Why does it sit beside the Qur’an?
English: The Qur’an gives the command and the Sunnah usually gives the method. "Establish the prayer" appears again and again; how many units, when, and what to say in them comes from watching him. The Qur’an itself instructs Muslims to take what the Messenger gives them.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I covered, and is the place clean?
English: Am I covered, and is the place clean?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I covered, and is the place clean?
English: The Qur’an tells people to take their adornment at every place of prayer, so dress as you would to meet someone you respect. Your clothes and the ground you pray on should be clean. A carpet, a towel or a mat is fine; a prayer mat is convenient, not required.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I covered, and is the place clean?
English: How much has to be covered differs a little between men and women and is set out in the clothing guide. Ordinary loose clothes cover it for most people.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I in wudu?
English: Am I in wudu?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I in wudu?
English: Wudu is the short wash before prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said the prayer of someone who has broken it is not accepted until they wash again. One wudu covers several prayers. It lasts until something breaks it, and the wudu guide sets out what does and what only feels as though it does.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Do I have to say the intention?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: The intention is a thought, not a sentence: knowing which prayer you are about to pray. You do not say it out loud, and you do not need a formula. If you are standing on a mat about to pray Maghrib, you have already intended it.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Some people are taught to say the intention aloud. Scholars differ on whether that is recommended, and nobody holds that the prayer fails without it.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Most of this is agreed and only one part of it is open. The imams agree that the place of the intention is the heart and that the prayer never asks you to speak it, so that is not one side of an argument. What they differ on is whether voicing it is recommended. Ibn Taymiyyah, who records both views, reports that scholars among the followers of Abu Hanifah, ash-Shafi`i and Ahmad held it recommended as a way of making the intention firmer, and that scholars among the followers of Malik and Ahmad held it is not, because neither the Prophet ﷺ nor his Companions did it; he takes the second view. This note used to give the first row as the majority and the second as a minority, which counted scholars nobody has counted and put an agreed point on one side of a disagreement. If you were taught to say it, saying it harms nothing.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Scholars of the school held that voicing the intention is recommended, as a way of making it firmer. The same view is found among Shafi`i and Hanbali scholars.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Scholars of the school held that voicing it is not recommended, since neither the Prophet ﷺ nor his Companions did it. The same view is found among Hanbali scholars.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: Is it the right time?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: Each prayer has a window, and you pray inside it rather than whenever you like, and the Qur’an calls prayer a decree of specified times. The Pray tab works the times out from where you are, on the phone, so you do not have to calculate anything.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: If your local mosque prints a timetable and it differs from the app by a few minutes, follow the mosque.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: The app works the times out from the position of the sun, which is arithmetic. A mosque timetable is a decision: which twilight angle to use for Fajr and Isha, whether to round to the nearest five minutes, whether to hold Isha back in summer so people can get there. Both are honest answers to the same question and they land a few minutes apart. Praying with the congregation you actually pray with matters more than the arithmetic, and the differences are almost always small enough that either time falls inside the window anyway. The one place it is worth checking is high summer in a northern country, where Fajr and Isha can crowd together and mosques handle it in noticeably different ways.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Which way do I face?
English: Which way do I face?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Which way do I face?
English: Muslims face the Kaʿbah in Mecca, and the Qur’an gives that instruction directly. The Qibla screen in this app points the way from where you are. If you cannot work it out, on a plane or in an unfamiliar place, face your best guess and pray; that is accepted.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — Am I qualified to say anything?
English: Am I qualified to say anything?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — Am I qualified to say anything?
English: To pass on what you actually know, yes. The Prophet ﷺ said to convey from him even a single sentence — which is a low bar deliberately, and it is a bar about accuracy rather than about credentials. What you are not qualified to do is answer questions you have not been taught the answer to, and the difference between those two is the whole of this page.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What do I say when I do not know?
English: What do I say when I do not know?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What do I say when I do not know?
English:
"I don’t know." Then, if you can: "let’s find out." That is a complete answer, it is honest, and it is what scholars say constantly — the ones worth listening to say it more often than anyone.

The temptation is to fill the gap, because being asked feels like being trusted and saying nothing feels like letting somebody down. It is not. Guessing at a ruling for somebody who will act on it is a considerably worse outcome than a pause.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What do I say when I do not know?
English: Watch for the question that is really about somebody’s specific situation — a marriage, money, family. Those need a person who can ask questions back, and that is rarely you.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What if I know the answer differs?
English: What if I know the answer differs?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What if I know the answer differs?
English:
Say so. "There is more than one view on that, and mine is what my mosque follows" is more useful to a beginner than a confident single answer, because it prepares them for the day somebody tells them otherwise.

This is the thing most likely to have been done TO you, and the easiest not to pass on.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What is actually worth passing on?
English: What is actually worth passing on?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — What is actually worth passing on?
English:
The things nobody told you. What happens in the first ten minutes at a mosque. That a short prayer counts. That your name stays. That the guilt about the years before is not evidence of anything.

Those are not advanced knowledge and they do not need a scholar. They are the things that were invisible to everybody who could have told you, and you are the only person likely to think of them.

Where it appears: When someone asks you — Why would anyone ask me?
English: Why would anyone ask me?

Where it appears: When someone asks you — Why would anyone ask me?
English: Because you remember not knowing, and almost nobody else in the room does. Somebody raised Muslim cannot tell you what is confusing about wudu, because it was never confusing to them. You can. That is a real thing to have, and it arrives at about year two whether you feel ready or not.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Is this Islam or is it their culture?
English: Is this Islam or is it their culture?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Is this Islam or is it their culture?
English:
Sometimes it is culture, and it is entirely fair to ask which. A useful question, asked plainly and without edge: **is that required, or is that how it is done where you are from?** Most people answer it honestly, and the ones who cannot were not going to be a good source anyway.

The five categories are worth having in your head for exactly this — much of what arrives as a rule is a recommendation, and some of it is a habit.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Is this Islam or is it their culture?
English: Being told the app or a book is wrong is also normal. Ask what it should say instead and where that comes from — that is not rude, it is the ordinary way this is discussed.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What if they were unkind about it?
English: What if they were unkind about it?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What if they were unkind about it?
English:
Then they were wrong about the manner, whatever they were right about in substance. Being correct does not license being harsh, and a religion whose Prophet ﷺ was described as gentle does not hand anybody a right to humiliate a stranger at prayer.

You are allowed to be hurt by it. What is worth not doing is concluding that the room, or the religion, is what that person was.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What if they were unkind about it?
English: If a particular mosque is consistently like this, try another one. They differ enormously, and moving is not a failure of patience.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What should I actually say?
English: What should I actually say?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — What should I actually say?
English:
"Thank you, I will look into it." That is a complete answer, it is true, and it ends the exchange without agreeing or arguing. You do not owe a defence of what you were doing, you do not have to explain that you are new, and you certainly do not have to debate it in a prayer hall.

Then look into it, once, when you are calm — and if two answers stay standing, follow the one your mosque follows.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why did someone correct me in front of everyone?
English: Why did someone correct me in front of everyone?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why did someone correct me in front of everyone?
English:
Because it will happen, and it is worth being ready rather than winded. Somebody will tell you your feet are wrong, your hands are in the wrong place, or that what you just did is not how it is done — usually in the middle of a room, usually meaning well, and usually with no idea that you have been Muslim for six weeks.

It is not a judgement on whether you belong there. It is a mosque doing the thing mosques do, and it happens to people who have prayed for forty years.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why do two people tell me opposite things?
English: Why do two people tell me opposite things?

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why do two people tell me opposite things?
English:
Almost always because they are following different schools of thought, and both are describing their own correctly. Where to put your hands, whether to say the intention aloud, how many times to wipe — these are places where the scholarship genuinely differs, and has for a thousand years.

Neither of them is lying to you and neither is making it up. You have walked into an old disagreement that nobody bothered to explain first.

Where it appears: When someone corrects you — Why do two people tell me opposite things?
English: That the schools differ on details of practice, within Sunni Islam, is not itself controversial. This app teaches one clear way because a first-timer needs a path — and it marks the places where a difference is one you will actually meet.

Where it appears: When someone dies — How do I pray the funeral prayer?
English: How do I pray the funeral prayer?

Where it appears: When someone dies — How do I pray the funeral prayer?
English:
You stand in a row and follow the imam, and you stay standing the whole way through — there is no bowing and no prostration in it, which surprises almost everybody the first time. He says **Allāhu akbar** four times, and between them there are quiet supplications. Then salām, and it is finished.

If you do not know the words, stand with them and say nothing. Following in silence is not a failure to participate.

Where it appears: When someone dies — How do I pray the funeral prayer?
English: Four takbīrs, standing, without rukūʿ or sujūd is agreed across the schools. What is said quietly between them is where they differ in detail.

Where it appears: When someone dies — How do I pray the funeral prayer?
English: You do not need wudu to attend, but you do to pray it — the same as any prayer.

Where it appears: When someone dies — Should I go if I did not know them?
English: Should I go if I did not know them?

Where it appears: When someone dies — Should I go if I did not know them?
English: Yes, and it is one of the few things in this religion that is straightforwardly encouraged for a stranger. The Prophet ﷺ described a reward for whoever attends until the prayer, and more for whoever stays until the burial. Turning up to a janāzah for somebody you never met is an ordinary thing to do.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What actually happens at a janāzah?
English: What actually happens at a janāzah?

Where it appears: When someone dies — What actually happens at a janāzah?
English: Quickly, and with very little ceremony. The body is washed and wrapped, a short prayer is prayed over it — usually at a mosque, often straight after one of the daily prayers — and it is buried, normally within a day. There is no open casket, no music, and no long service.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What actually happens at a janāzah?
English: It moves fast. If you hear in the morning, the burial may be that afternoon — that is normal and not a sign anybody is rushing.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say to the family?
English: What do I say to the family?

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say to the family?
English:
Very little, and that is correct. "May Allah have mercy on them" is enough, and so is nothing at all. Sit with people, make tea, take the children out. Grief in Islam is not silenced — crying is not a failing, and nobody has to pretend to be composed.

What is avoided is the loud, staged kind of mourning, and any suggestion that the family should be over it.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say to the family?
English: Do not tell somebody their loss was a test they passed, or that it was for the best. Neither is comfort, and both are said constantly.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say when I hear?
English: What do I say when I hear?

Where it appears: When someone dies — What do I say when I hear?
English:
The words people say on hearing that someone has died are from the Qur’an: **Innā li-llāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn** — to Allah we belong, and to Him we return. Say it quietly, to yourself. It is not a performance and nobody is waiting to hear it.

You say it for anyone. It is not reserved for Muslims, and it is not reserved for people you were close to.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What if the person who died was not Muslim?
English: What if the person who died was not Muslim?

Where it appears: When someone dies — What if the person who died was not Muslim?
English: Then this page is not the shape of it, and you are still allowed to grieve them, attend, and be with your family. What you may and may not take part in depends on what the funeral involves, and that is a question for somebody who knows both your family and the situation — not for an app.

Where it appears: When someone dies — What if the person who died was not Muslim?
English: Ask someone before the day rather than on it. This is one of the questions imams are asked most and least surprised by.

Where it appears: When you are angry — Is it weak to hold back?
English: Is it weak to hold back?

Where it appears: When you are angry — Is it weak to hold back?
English: The opposite. The strong person, he ﷺ said, is not the one who wins a wrestling match; the strong one is the one who has hold of himself at the moment of anger. Nothing in this asks you to be timid or to let yourself be walked over. It relocates strength from the exchange to the self-control it took not to have it.

Where it appears: When you are angry — So am I sinning for feeling angry?
English: So am I sinning for feeling angry?

Where it appears: When you are angry — So am I sinning for feeling angry?
English: No. Anger arrives; you do not choose it, and there is anger in the Prophet’s own life over things that deserved it. What is being asked for is the gap between feeling it and acting on it — leaving the room, saying nothing for a minute, saying the words above. The instruction is about the second half, not the first.

Where it appears: When you are angry — What do I actually do in the moment?
English: What do I actually do in the moment?

Where it appears: When you are angry — What do I actually do in the moment?
English: Two men were arguing in front of the Prophet ﷺ until one of them was red in the face, and he said that he knew a sentence which, if the man said it, would take away what he was feeling: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shayṭān. It is short enough to say through clenched teeth, which is the point — it is not a reflection to sit down with, it is something to reach for while it is happening.

Where it appears: When you are angry — What do I actually do in the moment?
English: The narration ends with the man refusing to say it — "I am not mad." Anger argues that it is reasonable, and it is the one state in which advice feels like an insult. Knowing that in advance is most of the help.

Where it appears: When you are angry — What does this look like for me now?
English: A relative will say something about your religion that is wrong and said to wound. It will happen when you are tired, in front of other people, and about the thing you care most about. How you answer that is the only thing about Islam most of them will ever read closely — which is unfair, and true. You are allowed to end a conversation. You are not required to win it.

Where it appears: When you are angry — What does this look like for me now?; Thinking you are better — What does this look like for me now?; Wanting what someone else has — What does this look like for me now?; Doing it to be seen — What does this look like for me now?; Patience and gratitude — What does this look like for me now?
English: What does this look like for me now?

Where it appears: When you are angry — Why is this the advice he kept repeating?
English: Why is this the advice he kept repeating?

Where it appears: When you are angry — Why is this the advice he kept repeating?
English: A man came asking for advice and was told: do not become angry. He asked again, and got the same two words. Again, and again the same. It is the shortest instruction in the collections and it was given to somebody who wanted a whole programme — because anger is the point at which most people lose everything else they have learned.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — How is it received?
English: How is it received?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — How is it received?
English: The Prophet ﷺ described God as more pleased with a person’s repentance than someone would be who lost their camel in the desert and then found it. The image is not of a grudging pardon. It is relief and delight.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — Is it too late for me?
English: Is it too late for me?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — Is it too late for me?
English: The Qur’an addresses people who have wronged themselves and tells them not to despair of God’s mercy, because He forgives all sins. That verse is worth knowing early, because the thing most likely to end someone’s practice is not a sin. It is deciding afterwards that they are past helping.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What does repentance actually take?
English: What does repentance actually take?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What does repentance actually take?
English: Stopping, meaning it, and asking. There is no ritual, no witness, and nobody to confess to. You turn to God directly. The Qur’an calls it turning to Him with sincere repentance, and that is the whole procedure.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What if I do it again?
English: What if I do it again?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What if I do it again?
English: You repent again. People expect to fail once and be finished; that is not how it works, and a habit that takes a year to break took a year for everybody else too. Keep praying while you work on it. Stopping the prayer because you feel unworthy of it is the one move that makes things worse.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What if I do it again?
English: Nobody is owed an account of your sins. You do not have to tell an imam, a friend, or anyone at the mosque.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — How do I get to know Him?
English: How do I get to know Him?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — How do I get to know Him?
English: Through His names, rather than in the abstract, and you will meet them constantly.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — How do I get to know Him?
English: Learning a few is a gentler way in than trying to think about God in the abstract.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — Is Allah a different God?
English: Is Allah a different God?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — Is Allah a different God?
English: No. Allah is simply the Arabic word for God, and Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews use it when they pray.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — Is Allah a different God?
English: It has no plural and no gender, which is part of why Muslims keep the word rather than translating it.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What if I try to picture Him?
English: What if I try to picture Him?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What if I try to picture Him?
English: Any picture you form is wrong by definition, and you are not expected to form one.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What if I try to picture Him?
English: This is why Muslims do not depict God, and why you will not find images of Him anywhere in Islam.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What was said when the Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe God?
English: What was said when the Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe God?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What was said when the Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe God?
English: A short chapter of the Qur’an, and Muslims have taken it as the definition ever since.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Do Muslims worship him?
English: Do Muslims worship him?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Do Muslims worship him?
English: Muhammad ﷺ was born in Mecca around 570 CE and received the Qur’an over roughly twenty-three years. Muslims believe he is the last of a long line of prophets that includes Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa, or Abraham, Moses and Jesus. He is not divine and is not worshipped. He delivered the message; the message is from God.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What is the ﷺ after his name?
English: What is the ﷺ after his name?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What is the ﷺ after his name?
English: You will see ﷺ written after his name throughout this app and everywhere else. It stands for an Arabic phrase asking God to bless him and grant him peace. Muslims say it aloud out of respect whenever he is mentioned. Nobody will mind if you forget at first.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What was he like?
English: What was he like?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What was he like?
English: The Qur’an describes him as being of great character, and the people who lived with him described someone who never used foul or crude language and who taught that the best people are those with the best manners. Much of what Muslims try to imitate is not ritual at all. It is how he treated people.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Why follow him?
English: Why follow him?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Why follow him?
English: Because the Qur’an tells them to. It calls him an excellent example, and says that obeying him is obeying God. In practice this is very concrete: the Qur’an commands prayer without describing how, and the answer to "how" is that he said, "Pray as you have seen me praying."

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Why follow him?
English: Loving and following him is not the same as worshipping him. The distinction matters to Muslims and is worth being clear about early.

Where it appears: Why people differ — Do I have to pick one?
English: Do I have to pick one?

Where it appears: Why people differ — Do I have to pick one?
English:
Not on day one, and probably not for a long time. In practice most converts end up following whichever school the mosque they attend follows, which is a perfectly ordinary way to arrive at it and requires no decision at all.

What is worth avoiding is assembling your own from whichever answer is easiest in each case. Not because anybody is policing it, but because it stops being a considered position and becomes a preference wearing a scholar’s name.

Where it appears: Why people differ — Do I have to pick one?
English: If somebody asks which madhhab you follow and you have no answer, "I pray with my local mosque" is a complete one.

Where it appears: Why people differ — How much do they actually disagree about?
English: How much do they actually disagree about?

Where it appears: Why people differ — How much do they actually disagree about?
English:
Far less than the noise suggests. Nobody differs about the five prayers, the fast of Ramadan, or what is forbidden. The differences are in the detail of practice — where the hands rest, whether the intention is said aloud, how many times something is wiped — and in the harder edges of law.

If you learned to pray from this app and prayed behind an imam of any of the four, you would be praying correctly. That is worth knowing before somebody tells you otherwise.

Where it appears: Why people differ — How much do they actually disagree about?
English: That the four schools are all within Sunni Islam, and that following any of them is following Islam, is not itself a matter of dispute.

Where it appears: Why people differ — What is a madhhab?
English: What is a madhhab?

Where it appears: Why people differ — What is a madhhab?
English:
A school of legal reasoning. Four of them are followed today — Ḥanafī, Mālikī, Shāfiʿī and Ḥanbalī — named after scholars of the first centuries, and every one of them is Sunni. They are not denominations and not sects. They are four careful attempts at the same question: given the Qur’an and the Sunnah, what exactly follows?

Most Muslims you meet follow one, usually the one their country follows, and most of them have never thought about it — the way most people have never thought about which grammar they speak.

Where it appears: Why people differ — Which one does this app teach?
English: Which one does this app teach?

Where it appears: Why people differ — Which one does this app teach?
English:
One clear way, on purpose, because somebody learning to pray needs a path rather than a comparison table. Where a difference is one you will actually meet — at a mosque, from a friend, in a book — the app marks it and says what the other positions are, rather than pretending there is only one.

So when you see a note saying scholars differ here, that is not the app hedging. It is the app telling you in advance about a conversation you are going to have.

Where it appears: Why people differ — Why would there be four answers?
English: Why would there be four answers?

Where it appears: Why people differ — Why would there be four answers?
English:
Because the texts do not spell out every case, and reading them takes judgement. Two scholars can hold the same narration, agree it is authentic, and still reach different conclusions about what it obliges — one reads a command as binding, the other as strongly encouraged; one has a narration the other never received.

That is not a flaw that was later discovered. It was anticipated: the Prophet ﷺ said that a judge who strives to reach the right answer is rewarded even when he gets it wrong, and rewarded twice when he gets it right. A religion that rewards a wrong answer arrived at honestly is a religion that expects careful people to disagree.

Where it appears: Witr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Witr.

Where it appears: Witr — Is one really enough?
English: Is one really enough?

Where it appears: Witr — Is one really enough?
English: Yes. The Prophet ﷺ named five, three and one, and left the choice to the person praying, so one is a complete witr rather than a shortened version of something else. Most people pray three, and you will see that around you.

Where it appears: Witr — Is one really enough?
English: Start with one. It is the whole prayer, it takes a minute, and it is the version you are least likely to get wrong while you are learning.

Where it appears: Witr — Turn to your left
English: That is Witr complete.

Where it appears: Witr — What if I sleep through it?
English: Pray it before you go to bed. Leaving it to the end of the night is better, but only if you are actually going to be awake. It is meant to be the last thing you pray, not the thing you missed.

Where it appears: Witr — What if I sleep through it?; Fajr — What if I sleep through it?
English: What if I sleep through it?

Where it appears: Witr — Why an odd number?
English: Why an odd number?

Where it appears: Witr — Why an odd number?
English: Because that is what the word means, and it is what you finish the night on.

Where it appears: Work and money — How does Islam see work?
English: How does Islam see work?

Where it appears: Work and money — How does Islam see work?
English: There is no ideal of poverty here. The Prophet ﷺ said nobody has eaten better food than what he earned by his own hands, and noted that the Prophet Dawud ate from his own labour. The Qur’an tells people to disperse and seek God’s bounty as soon as the Friday prayer ends.

Where it appears: Work and money — What about interest?
English: What about interest?

Where it appears: Work and money — What about interest?
English: Riba, usually translated as interest or usury, is prohibited in the Qur’an in strong terms, and the Prophet ﷺ listed consuming it among the gravest sins. In practice this is what makes conventional mortgages, interest-bearing savings and most credit cards a live question for Muslims.

Where it appears: Work and money — What about interest?
English: If you already have a mortgage or a loan, you have not ruined anything and you do not have to solve it this month. Islamic finance options exist in many countries and vary a great deal. Scholars have discussed this in more detail, so get advice on your actual situation.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: What if my job touches something forbidden?

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: Directly producing or selling what is prohibited is the clear case. The Prophet ﷺ said the curse on wine falls on ten, its seller and the one who lives off its price among them. What is less clear is indirect involvement: a supermarket cashier who occasionally scans wine, a delivery driver, an accountant at a bank. That distance is exactly what scholars weigh.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: Scholars differ on how much distance from a prohibited thing is enough, so answers vary by how central it is to the job.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: The usual reasoning looks at whether the forbidden thing is the point of the work or incidental to it, at how much of your income depends on it, and at what leaving would cost you. Someone whose whole income is from selling alcohol is in a different position from someone who occasionally rings it through a till, and someone who cannot simply leave is in a different position again. This note used to set out two positions and attribute one to the majority and one to contemporary scholarship, which stated a count nobody has taken, and the first of them was not a disagreement at all, since the clear case is agreed. Where scholars actually differ is on the line, and the line moves with the facts, which is why the answer here is to describe your actual job to someone qualified rather than to read a general rule off a page.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: Do not quit your job the week you become Muslim. Find out what your options are first.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Finish

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: When you are done, say:

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: You are now ready to pray.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: If you are ever rushed or short of water, the four parts the Qur’an itself names are the face, the arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and the feet to the ankles. Once each is enough. Everything else here is the fuller way the Prophet ﷺ did it.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Schools differ over what else is strictly required beyond those four. The intention, keeping to the order, and washing without long pauses in between are each treated as a requirement in some schools and as a recommendation in others. Teaching the full method sidesteps the question entirely, which is why this guide does. Knowing the shorter version matters on the day you have half a bottle of water and a prayer to catch.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Intend in your heart that you are performing wudu to purify yourself for prayer, then say:

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: One wudu covers as many prayers as you like. It lasts until something breaks it, and only then do you wash again.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: What certainly breaks it: anything that leaves you from the front or the back, such as using the toilet or passing wind, and losing awareness, whether through sleep deep enough that you would not have noticed, fainting, or anything else that takes your senses away.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Bukhari 135 is the Prophet's ﷺ words that the prayer of someone who breaks their wudu is not accepted until they wash again. Abu Huraira, asked what breaking it meant, answered: passing wind. On sleep the wording is "the eyes are the drawstring of the backside, so whoever sleeps should perform wudu". Schools qualify that by how deeply and in what position, but all four agree that heavy sleep ends it, and all four agree that losing your senses another way, whether fainting, anaesthetic or being drunk, ends it too, which is why this note names that rather than only sleep.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Two more are handled differently by the schools: touching your own private parts, and skin contact with the opposite sex. If one of those happens and you are unsure, washing again takes a minute and settles it.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: The split is not carelessness. It is two authentic narrations pointing different ways. Busrah bint Safwan reports "whoever touches his penis should not pray until he performs wudu"; Talq ibn `Ali reports the Prophet ﷺ answering "is it anything other than a piece of him?" Tirmidhi grades both sound and records that the second is the position of the scholars of Kufa. On the opposite sex, the verse says "or you have touched women", and the argument is over whether that word means intercourse or ordinary contact; `A'isha reports that the Prophet ﷺ kissed her and prayed without washing again.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Neither of the two breaks wudu on its own.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Both break it where there is desire: the private parts touched deliberately with the palm, and contact with the opposite sex accompanied by desire.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Both break it regardless of intention: the private parts touched with the palm and no barrier, and skin contact with an adult of the opposite sex who is not a close relative.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Touching the private parts breaks it; contact with the opposite sex breaks it where there is desire.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend; Ghusl — Intend; Tayammum — Intend
English: Intend

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your mouth
English: Rinse your mouth

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your mouth
English: Take water into your mouth with your right hand, swill it around and spit it out. Three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your nose
English: Rinse your nose

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your nose
English: Sniff a little water into your nose with your right hand, then blow it out using your left. Three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your nose
English: Draw it up properly, unless you are fasting, in which case go gently.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your arms
English: Wash your arms

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your arms
English: Wash your right arm from the fingertips to just past the elbow, three times. Then the left, three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your arms
English: Right before left is the pattern for everything that comes in a pair.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your face
English: Wash your face

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your face
English: Wash your whole face three times, from your hairline to under your chin and from ear to ear.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your feet
English: Wash your right foot to just past the ankle, between the toes, three times. Then the left, three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your feet; Ghusl — Wash your feet
English: Wash your feet

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your hands
English: Wash both hands up to the wrists, three times, between the fingers.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your hands; Ghusl — Wash your hands
English: Wash your hands

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your ears
English: Wipe your ears

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your ears
English: With the same wetness, put your index fingers inside your ears and your thumbs behind them, and wipe. Once.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your head
English: Wipe your head

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your head
English: With wet hands, wipe over your head from the front to the back and return to the front. Once.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your head
English: Wiping, not washing, and once rather than three times.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What do I do when I walk in?
English: What do I do when I walk in?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What do I do when I walk in?
English: There will be a shoe rack by the door. Take your shoes off there and carry them in if the rack is full. Step in with your right foot. There are usually separate entrances or areas for men and women. Look for the signs, or ask; nobody minds being asked.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens afterwards?
English: What happens afterwards?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens afterwards?
English: People turn and greet whoever is beside them. Say salam back. Someone will very likely ask if you are new. This is the moment the whole trip is actually for, and it is worth staying ten minutes for it.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens in the prayer?
English: What happens in the prayer?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens in the prayer?
English: People stand shoulder to shoulder in straight lines, filling from the front. Stand in a line, follow the imam, and do what the row does. You do not say anything aloud and nobody is watching you.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What if I get something wrong?
English: What if I get something wrong?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What if I get something wrong?
English: Being a beat behind in the movements. Not knowing where to stand. Your phone going off. Asking a stranger what to do. Leaving straight after. Getting the words wrong under your breath.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What if I get something wrong?
English: Everyone in that room was new once, including the imam. Nobody is grading you, and the ones who notice you are new are almost always pleased about it.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What should I do before I go?
English: What should I do before I go?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What should I do before I go?
English: Do your wudu at home if you can. It is one less thing to work out when you arrive. Wear clean clothes that cover you from the navel to the knees at minimum; loose trousers and a long top are entirely normal. What a woman covers is no different here from anywhere else in front of men outside the family, and the clothing guide sets it out with the verses behind it.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — When should I go the first time?
English: When should I go the first time?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — When should I go the first time?
English: Friday midday is the busiest hour of the week. For a first visit, go for a normal prayer: Dhuhr in the early afternoon, or ʿIshaʾ at night. Fewer people, more room to watch what everyone else does.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — When should I go the first time?
English: Friday prayer is obligatory for men, so you will need to go eventually. It is easier once the building is already familiar.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — Where do I sit?
English: Where do I sit?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — Where do I sit?
English: Pray two short rakʿah before you sit down. It is what everyone does on entering. Then sit anywhere on the carpet. There is no reserved seating and no collection.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — Where do I sit?
English: If a prayer is already in progress, join the line where you are and follow the imam from wherever he has got to. When he finishes and gives salām, stand back up and pray the rakʿahs you missed on your own — that is what completes your prayer.

Where it appears: ʿAsr — What is ʿAsr?
English: What is ʿAsr?

Where it appears: ʿAsr — What is ʿAsr?
English: Four silent rakʿahs in the last stretch of the afternoon, prayed while the day is still busy — which is exactly why so much was said about it.

Where it appears: ʿAsr — Why does it matter so much?
English: Four narrations give this one afternoon prayer unusual weight.

Where it appears: ʿIsha — Is it hard to end the day with it?
English: Is it hard to end the day with it?

Where it appears: ʿIsha — Is it hard to end the day with it?
English: It is meant to be the easy one to skip — which is exactly what the Prophet ﷺ said about it: no prayer sits heavier on a hypocrite than ʿIsha and Fajr, and if people knew what was in them they would come crawling. Praying it is quietly deciding which kind of person the day ends as.

Where it appears: ʿIsha — What is ʿIsha?
English: What is ʿIsha?

Where it appears: ʿIsha — What is ʿIsha?
English: Four rakʿahs once night has settled — and prayed in congregation, it is counted like standing half the night in prayer.
